content.content:
It is a bright time for German democracy. After a period of struggle, inflation is finally under control, and the economy is expanding steadily. In foreign policy, we have reached agreements with the Western powers and the Soviet Union that might make genuine peace a reality.

Now, the task of Social Democracy is to prepare for the next election. The bourgeois-right government of Wilhelm Marx is unpopular, and we stand to gain. Perhaps the next government will have a socialist majority.
The current bourgeois-right government has fallen. The next elections are slated for May of this year.

A new Liberal Association has been gaining traction with funding from both parties, and are expected to open up state and local chapters and to draft a policy program. This seems to be the prelude to the founding of a new liberal party, but it's not certain if both parties will consent to this.

content.content: Troubled by the surge of far‑right populism and the emboldened left, Germany’s heavy‑industry financiers have begun quietly pressuring the KVP/DNVP and the DVP to discuss tighter cooperation. The industrialist backers hope that the two parties working closer together will help bolster their leverage in the Reichstag. Members in both the KVP/DNVP and DVP, notably Treviranus and Dingeldey, are optimistic about these potential meetings.After weeks of behind the scenes pressure, the KVP/DNVP and the DVP have formally begun a series of joint meetings aimed at coordinating legislative strategy in the Reichstag. While Treviranus and Dingeldey lead the talks with cautious optimism, reservations linger among the KVP/DNVP’s agrarian wing, who fear further influence from the city focused industrial interests in the DVP. The DVP’s moderate wing is similarly resistant, as they see this as another step away from Stresemann’s legacy.

After weeks of careful deliberation, the KVP/DNVP and the DVP have made unexpectedly rapid strides in aligning their party platforms and coordinating candidate selection. That momentum has put a formal merger squarely on the table. Treviranus and Dingeldey applaud the unprecedented unity, openly acknowledging that a full merger could be on the horizon. Both the DVP’s moderate wing and the KVP/DNVP’s agrarians are still voicing concerns, but find their resistance increasingly sidelined as the broader majority coalesces around deeper integration.

. They argue that this tax, primarily levied on businesses, is an unreasonable burden on job creators given the current economic crisis. Brüning now finds himself caught between appeasing big industry on one side and placating organized agriculture and Hindenburg on the right.

content.content: The Brüning cabinet has introduced the Eastern Aid Act, a policy aimed at relieving the debts of agricultural enterprises in the east—despite the significant financial burden it imposes. This measure directly contradicts Brüning’s broader strategy of economic recovery through budget austerity. To partially fund the policy, the government has retained outdated reparation taxes that became obsolete after the Young Plan. However, the lack of full funding for debt relief has frustrated many influential landowners, prompting them to take their complaints directly to Hindenburg, over whom they wield considerable influence.

Brüning’s decision to sideline the Reichstag and its parties from any meaningful role in shaping his fiscal and economic policies severely undermined the legitimacy of the bourgeois parties in the eyes of their traditional electorates, due to their powerlessness to dismantle his more repugnant policies. One clear example is the plight of civil servants, who have borne the brunt of salary cuts of approximately 20 percent, pushing many toward the Nazis. His deflationary and austerity measures deepened the economic crisis, radicalizing the very social groups upon which these moderate parties relied for electoral support. This has led to heightened tensions between Brüning and his supporting parties, some of whom are even threatening to abandon his coalition.

This is a clear retreat from the unabashed defense of liberal principles that had characterized Stresemann’s tenure as party chairman.

content.content: The Second Spanish Republic has been established, replacing the monarchy of Alfonso XIII. This follows municipal elections in which republican candidates scored significant victories, winning in all 41 provincial capitals. This has forced the king into exile and a new, young republic has been created.

They now claim to be 'correcting' their position by 'reducing the evaluation of fascism to its proper proportions', which means reverting back to their social fascist stance. To them, we are no different than the actual fascists.

Hugenberg's attempts to cultivate a Hitler-style personality have failed, as his upper-class elitism and arrogance leave him out of touch with ordinary people suffering from the economic crisis. Frustrated by his lack of charisma, a group of industrialists has even offered a large reward for anyone who can help depose him, convinced he is steering the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
toward disaster. Adding to his troubles, the economic depression has slashed revenues from his media empire, forcing him to cut the

content.content: The formation of the Austro-German customs union has prompted France to exert significant economic pressure on Austria. Leveraging its sizable influence over the Austrian economy, France is not only refusing to extend financial assistance to the country’s struggling major banks but is also deliberately withdrawing large sums of money, further destabilizing Austria's financial sector.

The major Austrian Bank Creditanstalt has declared bankruptcy, following French political and economic pressures aimed at undermining the plans for the Austro-German customs union. In that respect, they have certainly succeeded. We can only hope that this crisis does not spill over into Germany or, worse, spread across Europe.

content: Following Creditanstalt's bankruptcy, an event that has shaken international financial markets, investors are now rapidly withdrawing funds from German banks. Germany's heavy reliance on short-term foreign loans has turned Austria’s banking crisis into a direct threat to our own stability. In response, Reichsbank President

has implemented measures to curb capital flight by disincentivizing the transfer of money abroad. However, the effectiveness of these policies remains uncertain, and may cause unintended consequences.

content.content: Rumors have circulated regarding Center Party leader Ludwig Kaas's intention to resign, as he has privately expressed a desire to step down from his burdensome position. His frequent absences from Germany, often spent in Rome, have left his deputy leader Joos and parliamentary leader Brüning to effectively manage the party. Kaas also holds one of the worst attendance records in the Reichstag. However, Kaas has attributed his prolonged absences to poor health, and the considerable autonomy he has granted to his colleagues has quelled efforts to replace him with a more active, though controversial, leader.

content: The organizational malaise of the <span style="color: #D3C24D;">

In some urban areas, the party’s shift to the right is estimated to have cost it more than half of its former supporters. In states without a strong liberal tradition, the situation is so dire that even the local branches that had once championed the formation of the
the previous year all but recommended conceding defeat and dissolving the party entirely.

content.content: The first elections of the Second Spanish Republic has been held, with it a great victory for the Spanish Socialists and the Republican Left. Together, they've formed a government with Manuel Azaña as Prime Minister.

Great Britain has abandoned the Gold Standard! The short-lived naval mutiny, caused by pay cuts, led to panic on the London Stock Exchange and a run on the Pound. The British government then adopted this policy as a means to stimulate industrial exports without the harmful side effects of deflation, achieved through the devaluation of the Pound. Germany's top economic experts viewed this as an act of desperation that would ruin England’s banks and insurance companies. Germany's citizens' fear of inflation, along with the obligation to preserve the mark’s value at 0.358 grams of fine gold under the Young Plan, has prevented Reichsbank President

from abandoning the Gold Standard. However, with both the United States and Britain showing sympathies toward our request for more flexible regulations, perhaps this decision was ultimately made on economic grounds after all.

Most of their replacements are conservatives—many of them nationalists. The purge is particularly aimed at socialist provincial presidents and police officials. An estimated 69 republican officials have been stripped of their power. Safe to say, the democratic bulwark has been dismantled.

However, the Nazi leadership's enthusiasm quickly fades when President Hindenburg refuses to appoint
as Chancellor. Papen, deeply offended by Schleicher's apparent willingness to abandon him, has used his growing rapport with Hindenburg to undermine Schleicher’s influence over the President.
Following the results of the Reichstag elections, Papen and President Hindenburg met with
to hear his demands for the party’s participation in government.

requested to be appointed chancellor once again—a demand Hindenburg refused. Buoyed by their electoral triumph, the Nazis have now officially reneged on their earlier promises to tolerate Papen. Going forward, they will pursue an all-or-nothing strategy: the chancellorship for
Papen has released the contents of last week's conversations with

stormed into Hindenburg’s office to demand “total power over the state”—a violent one-party dictatorship—and was met with an angry rebuff from the president. This press release signals aims to signal the start of a counter-offensive against the Nazis. But now, no party is willing—or able—to follow the chancellor into open confrontation with the extremists. Even the Center Party finds
’s version of events more credible than Papen’s.
Coalition talks between the Center Party and
have continued, putting pressure on Papen to outmaneuver his former party in gaining the favor of the Nazis. Brüning, with permission from his party's leadership, has meet with the
's Strasser, promising support if he could convince
to govern via a parliamentary cabinet with Schleicher as Defense Minister and Goerdeler as the commissioner of Prussia.
Under pressure from their principal patron, General von Schleicher, the <span style="color: #0087DC;">

is compelled to support the unpopular Papen government—or risk losing Schleicher’s covert Reichswehr funding. Outraged by the party's backing of such an anti-social chancellor, the Christian Socials resign their positions in protest.
A follow-up meeting to last week’s discussion about a potential Black-Brown alliance, set up by Strasser, has resulted in
agreeing to delay the vote of no confidence against Papen.
also appeared to agree with Brüning’s other demands. Closer cooperation is expected in the near future, if both parties are genuine in their commitment to govern together via parliament.

content.content: Austria has obtained a League of Nations loan that is tied to a 20-year ban on Anschluss, but opposition from the Social Democrats and Greater German Party has stalled the law, before it finally is passed by a single vote.

content: The coalition talks between the Center Party and
have been called off, as Brüning grows increasingly uneasy about the grave risks involved. This decision is also influenced by his friend and our party member, Hilferding, who argued that the

would never restore parliamentary government. Hilferding also pointed out that many of Brüning's own party colleagues have fallen under Nazi influence, a fact confirmed when they all but agreed to impeach President Hindenburg in the planned deal. Hilferding also remains the only one in our party to advocate for toleration of Papen's cabinet as the only means to prevent a Nazi dictatorship. Brüning's goal is now to persuade the Nazis to give the Papen government 'a fair chance' to revive the economy.
The Center Party and its grassroots supporters are becoming increasingly demoralized, largely due to Brüning’s semi-secret negotiations with the

. Locally, party activists have faced the Nazis as violent thugs, disrupting rallies and intimidating opponents—far from the image of a potential coalition partner. Some activists are even taking up arms in self-defense, losing faith in their party and its leadership.

has publicly opposed the party’s recent vote of no confidence and the snap elections it triggered, warning that such moves would only erode the Nazis’ popular support and squander their only real chance to seize power. In response, an unofficial faction of about sixty Nazi Reichstag deputies has coalesced around Strasser—disillusioned by

content.content: General elections were held in Sweden, resulting in a great victory for Per Albin Hansson and his Social Democrats, who now govern in a minority government. The Swedish Social Democrats have embraced the concept of a 'people's home', a form of reformist socialism aimed at reducing class divides while working in the capitalist framework. Perhaps we should consider following their 'nordic' model?

The main proceedings in the case against Papen’s unconstitutional Reichsexekution of the Prussian government have begun, with a verdict expected in the coming weeks. Yet, the historically reactionary leanings of the judiciary place us at a clear disadvantage—despite support from the state governments of Bavaria and Baden, who have joined us in challenging the decree’s legality.

Chancellor of Austria Engelbert Dollfuß has used the "War Economy Enabling Act", a law passed during the days of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which allowed him to restructure the Creditanstalt without parliamentary approval. While the Austrian Social Democrats have protested, Dollfuß' actions are technically legal.

content: , in an attempt to revive their poll numbers, have outlined the concept of "national democracy," aiming to rekindle the nationalistic impulse that played such a crucial role in the German liberal movement. However, it is essentially a restatement of classical liberal ideology, tailored to appeal to a more nationalistic German middle class. The national democracy program also reaffirms the
's commitment to the Weimar Republic and recommends constitutional changes to strengthen it.
With its electoral alliance with the DNVP, the
's freedom of action has become increasingly constrained. Their rhetoric is aligning more closely with the
, now calling for the "liquidation of the Weimar system," an authoritarian overhaul of its constitution, and the withdrawal of power away from the masses.
Dingeldey and his associates are no longer content with merely renewing their electoral list connection with the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
. Instead, they pushed for a unified Rechtsblock of the

, and various industrialist and business organizations to provide cohesive support for Hindenburg and Papen. However, Hugenberg has shown utter indifference, refusing to commit to anything beyond a renewal of the electoral list connection.
President Hindenburg has once again attempted to sound out the Nazis after the recent election results, with
signaling his readiness to seek the support of other parties if he were to be made chancellor first. Calling
's bluff, the president offered to appoint him, but only if he could secure a working majority in the Reichstag and allow the president to pick the defense and foreign ministers himself. As expected,
declined Hindenburg's proposal and suggested instead that, with emergency powers, he could form a satisfactory government in no time. Convinced that
sought nothing less than a presidential chancellorship, Hindenburg withdrew him from consideration.
Following another disastrous result for the <span style="color: #D3C24D;">
, a group of six former Reichstag deputies and high-ranking party members informed

that if a party congress—specifically meant to dissolve the party—isn't held, they would leave. However, this call has not gained much support, and Carl Petersen, former <span style="color: #D3C24D;">
chairman, has used his mediation skills to prevent the dissidents from publicly announcing their break with the party.

content.content: Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt has defeated incumbent Republican President Herbert Hoover in a landslide in the United States presidential election. This is attributed by the Great Depression and Roosevelt's campaigning for a "New Deal", proposing expansive public works and government reform.
Rumors are circulating widely that General Schleicher intends to undermine the very chancellor he helped install. Among his contacts, he's already being referred to as the chancellor-designate.

content: to make one final attempt at forming a majority coalition. Reporting back the next day,
confirmed that no such majority could be assembled. His recommendation was blunt: the only way forward is for the President to dismiss Papen, as the Reichstag will never accept him as chancellor.

has suffered yet another crushing setback—this time in the local elections in Thuringia. The results show the party lost nearly a quarter of its vote share compared to the previous state election. While low turnout may be a factor, this and three other recent local elections have only reinforced the growing sense that the Nazis have peaked and are rapidly losing support.

content.content: Despite his ousting, Papen remains in far closer physical proximity to the President than the chancellor does. At Hindenburg’s personal request, he continues to reside in an apartment within the Interior Ministry building—just steps from Hindenburg’s own quarters—while Schleicher lives miles away in a private residence. This arrangement has enabled Papen to scheme full-time, without attracting public attention.

Once a close ally, Oskar von Hindenburg has become an implacable enemy of the new chancellor—reportedly over a tasteless joke that wounded his pride beyond forgiveness. In Prussian times, such insults could end in duels; this time, the fallout may claim the life of the Republic. Two members of the Camarilla now harbor intense hostility toward Schleicher, and are working to sway the President into reconsidering his appointment.

Shortly after Schleicher’s appointment, the Western Allies, following protracted negotiations at the Geneva Disarmament Conference, conceded in principle to Germany’s right to equality in arms. The practical terms of this concession remain unclear, but in Schleicher’s view, it opens the path toward establishing an official militia service.

During Schleicher's addresses to the nation, one central theme rings clear: "Create Work!" He has revived efforts to resettle the urban unemployed on rural homesteads carved from bankrupt estates in the sparsely populated East. Although the Reichstag remains dissolved and he cannot legislate, he has publicly opposed Papen’s changes to the unemployment insurance system, presenting himself as a proponent of neither capitalism nor socialism. His ideological ambiguity has earned him the nickname "social general"—a label he embraces, claiming it aligns with the army’s tradition of solidarity between officers and soldiers.

content: 's resurgence in the polls has led Dingeldey to become overconfident, unequivocally supporting Papen, then Schleicher, and even forming a parliamentary faction with the various splinter parties between it and the
. While this move has bolstered their influence, it has alienated Hugenberg and the
, on whom they still depend on as of their electoral alliance.
For some odd reason, von Schleicher came to believe that nothing came of
’s attempts to be appointed parliamentary chancellor simply because the man didn’t “at the bottom of his heart” want the office. By

, this suspicion had become a firm conviction; he repeatedly confided to journalists and his cabinet that the man simply doesn’t really want power. This belief is leading to Schleicher overestimating his chances of securing <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
Heavy electoral losses for the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

in local elections have further reinforced the disillusionment of the voters who have brought the movement to prominence, many who joined and donated to the party expecting to receive the spoils of victory are beginning to despair, withdrawing their donations. Admission fees for rallies, once a major source of income at the local level, have collapsed despite steep price reductions.

's failure to gain the chancellorship or enter government to constructively relieve Germany's economic woes has caused further frustration among the movement. However, Nazi leaders are quick to suppress any leaks of dissent or rumors of decline to the public.
The global economy is on the upswing—and with it, the erosion of the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
continues. The republican police force surveilling the

in Munich has noted clear signs of disintegration. Resignations are occurring daily, membership dues arrive irregularly, and expulsions over indebtedness are increasingly common. Every branch of the party appears run down. As for morale, the police report observed: “The view that the peak has passed and favorable prospects are missed is commonly held among many members.”
Schleicher still clings to the illusionary hope that the now powerless Strasser might somehow persuade
to allow Nazi participation in his cabinet, now that Strasser has returned from vacation. Strasser’s absence from the public eye has unsettled

, who now fears potential backroom plots to fracture the party—especially given the eagerness of Strasser’s remaining loyalists to do just that. In reality, all Strasser does is to warn former chancellor Brüning that Papen has arranged a secret meeting with Hitler—set to take place within a week or two—to conspire against their mutual enemy: Schleicher.

's financial situation is becoming dire. Increasingly, equipment and supplies are being acquired on credit—credit that's already drying up under the weight of the party's existing debts. Tensions have begun to flare between the

and the party leadership over how to divide dwindling donations, with some members resorting to begging in the streets or organizing lotteries to scrape together funds. One more election, and the party could face a full-blown financial crisis.

Despite promising President Hindenburg not to publicly criticize his favored former chancellor, Schleicher has done just that in a bid to distance himself from the deeply unpopular Papen. Hindenburg, displeased by the breach of trust, grows increasingly estranged from Schleicher. Papen, for his part, has shown little outward hostility toward his ouster—carefully masking his resentment and thirst for revenge beneath a façade of cordiality. In the meantime, Hindenburg has quietly authorized him to serve as his secret liaison to

content.content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has grown frustrated with the chancellor after a request for intervention to clear bureaucratic obstacles was flatly rejected. His ambitious projects remain stalled. Gereke, disillusioned, has confided his disappointment to his close friend—none other than Oskar von Hindenburg.

content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has had his project accelerated after his request for the chancellor to intervene and clear bureaucratic obstacles was approved.
Schleicher's eagerness to follow through on his promise to satisfy the unions and the <span style="color: #c00000;">
, and to put additional pressure on the
before their electoral base returns to work, has driven this decision.
Schleicher's eagerness to fulfill his promise to the unions, and to curb the growing <span style="color: #700000;">
vote share among radicalized workers, has motivated the move.

content.content: The disastrous state of the German economy has made rearmament a pipe dream, and Schleicher is eager to get it back on track.

The campaign for the Landtag elections in the microscopically small Free State of Lippe has begun, with the Nazis investing a substantial amount of resources to sway just a hundred thousand voters. However, despite its small size, a victory here could dispel the growing belief that the Nazis are on the brink of a catastrophic decline.

content: At a private dinner with journalists, Chancellor von Schleicher repeatedly expressed confidence that the Nazi leader would eventually come around to tolerating his cabinet—despite

’s public affirmations of an all-or-nothing course. This, even as Schleicher made clear he would dissolve the Reichstag if needed, a move he believes would cost the Nazis further seats (though he seeks to avoid such a step, fearing the
would benefit most from their collapse). “They’ll soon be eating out of my hand,” were the chancellor’s exact words that evening. What Schleicher fails to grasp is that
is no ordinary politician. He will not respond rationally, nor prudently, to Strasser’s break or to the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
’s electoral collapse. He believes destiny is on his side.

Chancellor von Schleicher and his press secretary have deliberately “leaked” plans to appoint Strasser as Vice Chancellor, Interior Minister, and Minister-President of Prussia, alongside naming the Center Party labor leader Stegerwald as Labor Minister. The Agriculture and Economics Ministries were reportedly reserved for Hugenberg himself. It’s highly likely this is a bluff—an attempt to pressure the
into dropping its total opposition, lest they risk being sidelined entirely.
With Dingeldey's pretentiousness, fueled by the <span style="color: #C0A054;">

's uptick in polling, elevating it to the lead party on the "moderate" Right, Hugenberg is growing increasingly irritated by their independence and seeks to terminate their electoral alliance if new elections are called. While the
still hopes to renew the alliance, they begin exploring the possibility of an accommodation with the

and the bourgeois parties as a safeguard against near-certain annihilation if Hugenberg severs ties. Meanwhile, the DNV (German National Association), a non-partisan organization aiming to consolidate the German middle, is starting to repair its relations with the liberals after already securing the support of the non-liberal right, with politicians like Treviranus.

content.content: Von Schleicher's bluffs—such as proposing a cabinet that includes both Stegerwald and Hugenberg—have lost all credibility. The Center Party has publicly ruled out Stegerwald serving alongside Hugenberg, a notorious enemy of organized labor. Moreover, the leak about the President’s meeting with Strasser has led to a permanent break between the Nazi leader and Schleicher, ending any hope that Strasser might persuade him to support a cabinet involving Schleicher. His contradictory tactics and careless remarks have only deepened mistrust and furthered his political isolation. He only now condemns efforts to postpone elections—despite having supported the idea just a week earlier.

With progress stalled across nearly all sectors, Schleicher has attempted to shift focus by bringing the issue of rearmament back into the public eye. He announced plans to establish a compulsory militia within a year, alongside a renewed commitment to arming the Reichswehr with heavy weaponry and instituting universal conscription. However, the impact of this intended public relations triumph is minimal, as news of Schleicher’s political setbacks dominates public attention.

Having failed to extract concessions from the chancellor to turn Germany into a dictatorship, the more radical elements within his party have pressured him into adopting an all-out opposition to Schleicher. A strongly worded resolution has been released, accusing him of "vacillation" in his willingness to "reform" the constitution. Furthermore, his initiative to restart peasant homesteads on bankrupt eastern estates has drawn the ire of conservative elites. With the next vote of no confidence looming, it may well come down to Schleicher versus the entire chamber.
The Rubicon has been crossed, and Schleicher stands on the other side. (keep in mind, all future content is highly speculative)

content: The Nazi Party is in total disarray, and the
—the most rebellious faction—has been the first to fall. Ernst Röhm
's direction, has been quietly scheming in recent days.

content.content: Dollfuß has abused his powers given in the "War Economy Enabling Act" to crack down on the workers in a railroad strike, which has resulted in all three presidents of parliament resigning amid a crucial vote. This crisis presented a perfect opportunity for Dollfuß to abolish the parliamentary system and restrict democratic rights, such as the freedom of the press and public protests. Another democracy has fell to authoritarianism.

Dollfuß's Austrofascist dictatorship has banned the Austrian Communists and the paramilitary of the Austrian Social Democrats, the Republican Protection League. He has also established the Fatherland Front, a party promoting a far-right fascist and corporate ideology.

content: The Spanish Socialists and the Republican Left have suffered an overwhelming defeat at the hands of the right wing

content.content: The Austrian Civil War has begun and ended in a matter of three days, fought between the Republican Protection League and Austria's Austrofascist regime, resulting in a defeat for the socialists across the border. The uprising was sparked by efforts to suppress the remnants of the Austrian Social Democrats and their paramilitary wing. However, the poorly coordinated and weakened movement was swiftly crushed by the army. Perhaps things would have gone more differently if they have taken up arms earlier.

With our policy of land reform, we are acquiring farmland from large estates, and giving the land to farmworkers' associations and small peasants. This policy has especially earned us the ire of President Hindenburg and his inner circle.

The pause in reparation payments, a budgetary surplus, and a struggling economy have created the conditions necessary to persuade both the Brüning cabinet and many economic experts that a stimulus plan is essential. The economy has hit rock bottom, deflation is in its damaging second phase, and the Lautenbach Plan is considered crucial for a rapid 'ignition' of the German economy, especially as reparations have already been paused. However, due to the German public's fear of inflation, announcing any dramatic expansion of the money supply has proven impossible. As a result, the Reichsbank is forced to scale back the plan to avoid any potential scandal that could threaten the Brüning government.

Labor Minister Adam Stegerwald and Finance Minister Hermann Dietrich have devised a plan to allocate a billion dollars for public works, along with efforts to reduce 'sticky' wages to restore investor confidence. The plan also includes the purchasing of foreign debts to increase liquidity, expanding credit, and reducing interest rates. The deficit generated by these measures is also somewhat offset by the need to pay less unemployment benefits. With these measures, money is beginning to flow once again into the German economy.

content: With Brüning focused on securing a foreign policy victory, the
's Labor Minister Adam Stegerwald and the

's Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Hermann Dietrich have been developing a job creation program. However, given the state of the national budget, such a program was not feasible without either severe welfare cuts or a breakthrough on reparations—delaying action until now due to fears of public backlash.
Dietrich has since proposed raising 1.4 billion Reichsmarks through a bond issue and secured Reichstag authorization for it.

content.content: However, the Reichsbank remains hesitant to support the plan financially, at least until the reparations question is settled at Lausanne in the coming months. As a result, the cabinet has scaled back Dietrich’s proposal, allocating only 135 million Reichsmarks and introducing additional austerity measures in the next emergency decree. The decree’s main feature is the creation of a new "Voluntary Labor Service" brigade, tasked with draining swamps and digging artificial lakes—at subminimum wages.

With reparations now resolved at Lausanne, the Reichsbank feels more comfortable authorizing spending. The decree’s centerpiece is the creation of a new "Voluntary Labor Service" brigade, tasked with draining swamps and digging artificial lakes—at subminimum wages.
Should Lausanne bring success, full funding for Dietrich’s program may still follow. Brüning just has to survive until then.

Despite Brüning’s longstanding belief that public works should follow the bottoming out of the depression, it appears he now sees that moment as having arrived—with the global recovery and the abolition of German reparations. Still, inflationary fears among the public have constrained any major expansion of the money supply, and the industrialists within the coalition have fought tooth and nail to gut the bill’s more expensive provisions. Fortunately, their votes are not required to pass it.

This marks a real turning point, and along with the abolishment of reparations, the radicalizing effects of sky-high unemployment and the Versailles Treaty are diminished. The set of conditions that have enabled the Nazis's meteoric rise begins to unravel, depriving them of the fuel that once drove their ascent.

content.content: Paul von Hindenburg has passed away at age 86.

Even though he was a manifestation of Prussian militarism and monarchism, he still led the nation through difficult times, without destroying democracy. It could always have been worse.

With the passing of Hindenburg, it seems as if an era of history is closing. The worst years of crisis are over, and Nazism's days are numbered. Perhaps Germany will finally enter into a new era of genuine peace...

content.content: The influx of Protestant conservatives into the Center Party has rendered Jakob Kaiser’s leadership untenable. In a decisive internal vote of no confidence, Kaiser has been ousted—replaced by Stegerwald ally and long-serving Mayor of Cologne, Konrad Adenauer. Adenauer seeks to carry forward Stegerwald’s vision: transforming the party into the dominant force of the German Right.

Unsurprisingly, this development has sparked outrage among the Christian Left and Kaiser’s supporters, many of whom have resigned their posts in protest. The party’s close ties to left-leaning unions have been severely strained, plunging the organization into temporary disarray as labor-aligned factions voice their anger.

content.content: Following the disastrous fallout from the Banking Crisis, Brüning has successfully managed to secure key concessions from the Western Allies regarding debts and Germany's economic maneuverability. However, Germany's economic crisis continues to worsen, and the Beneduce Report has stated that Germany cannot afford reparations payments in the foreseeable future. The British government has invited the Western Allies to participate in an international reparations congress in Lausanne, as per the recommendations of the bankers.

With the moratorium on reparations in place, there is considerable uncertainty regarding what will happen to Germany's reparations burden once it expires. Brüning argues that this uncertainty has stifled investor confidence and hindered Germany's recovery from the economic crisis. The dire state of German finances has also contributed to this, with the Beneduce Report painting a bleak picture of Germany's ability to repay reparations in the foreseeable future. The British government has invited the Western Allies to participate in an international reparations congress in Lausanne, as per the recommendations of the bankers.

This is where the dilemma arises: France's government cannot discuss any permanent revision of the Young Plan until after their elections in May. Brüning faces a choice: he can either push for a prolongation of the moratorium on reparations for another three years, or he can wait until June for a potential complete abolition of reparations.

content.content: We have observed that the Nazis are encountering clear ecological limits to their continued growth, particularly due to their inability to secure a decisive breakthrough into the Catholic or working-class voting blocs. This pattern has emerged across Germany, and with their adamant opposition to entering government without absolute power, they are destined to fizzle out.

papen_cabinet_1.papen.title: Papen announces his goals to the nation.

content.content: In his first radio address to the German people, Papen laid out the ideological direction of his government. He denounced previous administrations for steering Germany toward "state socialism," blaming them for the "moral decay" wrought by an "unholy class war" and "cultural Bolshevism." He also condemned the transformation of Germany into a welfare state and seeks to reverse our progress over the years.

content: As Vorwärts puts it, this marks "a unique declaration of class war from above." The <span style="color: #c00000;">
—after months of decline, are poised for resurgence as the battle between the barons and the people begins. Moreover, if the
were to back this cabinet, it could trigger a collapse in their popular support.

content.content: With no progress made on securing Nazi toleration of the cabinet, and Papen still unable to survive a Reichstag vote when the chamber reconvenes, Schleicher has advised the chancellor to resign in order to calm the national mood. This would allow the President to seek a broader base of support without Papen at the helm.

However, Papen’s cabinet continues to function in a caretaker role, and little has changed fundamentally. As Papen has stated to his cabinet, none of this matters, as Hindenburg remains "firmly resolved to take all measures that might become necessary" to support him.

papen_cabinet_2.papen.title: The decree is signed by President Hindenburg.

content.content: The decree confirms the overtly anti-social character of the so-called “cabinet of barons,” and has ignited fury across the working class. With nearly two-thirds of the country now irrevocably hostile to the chancellor, it is politically suicidal for any party outside the reactionary right to support him without suffering severe electoral consequences.

papen_cabinet_2.title: Papen's First Emergency Decree
papen_cabinet_2.subtitle: A virtual abolishment of unemployment insurance!

content: Papen has unveiled his first emergency decree—one that keeps most of Brüning’s planned austerity measures but strips away the system of peasant homesteads. Most egregiously, it subjects all recipients of unemployment insurance to a means test after just six weeks. In effect, the system has been dismantled—radicalizing the proletariat, especially toward the <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: Unlike Brüning, who at least aimed to share the burdens of austerity across classes, Papen’s decree openly targets the working poor. Unsurprisingly, the gutting of the welfare state has triggered a spike in unemployment and a sharp dip in the stock market. As ever, Germany finds itself with no shortage of problems.

content.content: With his last hope for salvaging power extinguished and all but one minister turning against him, Papen is left with no viable path forward—resign now, or be crushed by the Reichstag later in the week.

Our grassroots party members are highly critical of our decision. Many party branches have increased their agitation against our parliamentary fraction, especially after we opposed the construction of the first ship in favor of food for children.

papen_cabinet_4.title: Decree Against Political Terror
papen_cabinet_4.subtitle: Papen attempts to combat the political violence he has enabled.

content.content: In an attempt to combat the common-place violence on the streets, that had particularly escalated days before the federal elections, a new decree has been issued to drastically streamline the judicial process in death penalty cases, which now includes politically motivated killings, and limiting the right of appeal. New special local courts are also created to fast track the prosecution of the most heinous of crimes.
Yet another disgraceful capitulation to the Nazis. Still, their shameless defense of convicted murderers may alienate voters and cost them dearly at the next election.

papen_cabinet_8.title: The 'Potempa Five' Are Pardoned!
papen_cabinet_8.subtitle: Murder excused in the name of politics.

content: In a bid to win Nazi support for his government, Papen and his Justice Minister have bowed to pressure and commuted the murderers' sentences, using his power as Prussia's Reichskommissar. The hope is that the
will back Papen in the upcoming confidence vote—but this capitulation has only strengthened the Nazis, laying bare the government's unwillingness—or inability—to confront them.

papen_cabinet_9.title: Papen Drafts Sweeping Amendments to the Constitution!
papen_cabinet_9.subtitle: Despite his extreme unpopularity, the chancellor has ordered his cabinet to begin drafting sweeping constitutional amendments.

content.content: As part of Papen’s previously announced ambition to create a “New State”—a reform of the constitution aimed at transforming Germany into a dictatorship reminiscent of the former Kaiserreich—the continued political deadlock has led him to pursue changes to the system itself. Lacking both popular support and a parliamentary majority, it's unclear how Papen would institute such changes. Nonetheless, such a move would almost certainly provoke civil war—one the Reichswehr is in no position to easily win.

Papen's increasing independence and assertiveness, distancing himself from Schleicher's control, has alarmed the latter, who had previously sought to manipulate him. His open calls for dictatorship, along with the risks involved in keeping such an unpopular chancellor by circumventing the constitution, would unite the legions of organized labor against the government—something Schleicher is anxious to avoid. After all, a civil war would severely impede Germany's rearmament.

title: At least

content.content: We’ve seen a slight decrease in unemployment—small, but in a depression this deep, any break from Brüning’s deflationary orthodoxy is a welcome change.

The following day, however, Papen issues a decree allowing employers to undercut wages set by collective bargaining agreements when hiring new workers, instantly sparking outrage among the socialist and Christian trade unions.

papen_cabinet_7.title: Emergency Ordinance for the Reactivation of Economy
papen_cabinet_7.subtitle: Tax relief for the rich and businesses.

content.content: Emergency Ordinance for the Reactivation of Economy

Papen has taken the initiative on economic matters, using the funds generated by the gutting of the unemployment insurance program to finance tax cuts for the wealthy and their businesses. This has solidified the backing of the industrial elite behind his chancellorship, but further cements his image as a chancellor for the barons.
However, it does help draw bourgeois sympathies into the cabinet, as many upper-class members of the Center and various bourgeois parties applaud his effort toward constructive policy.

content: The Reichstag has reconvened for the first time since the election, with a significantly larger contingent of <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

members now present. The immediate issue at hand is the election of the President of the Reichstag. While the position has traditionally been a procedural one, it has taken on heightened importance under Papen's presidential government, given the President's authority to influence the agenda and adjourn sessions.
By long-standing custom, the role is granted to the largest parliamentary delegation. That delegation is now the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
. The Center Party holds the balance of power. Will they uphold tradition and hand a key parliamentary post to an openly anti-constitutional party?

papen_cabinet_reichstag_2.title: Emergency Decree to Suspend Parliament?
papen_cabinet_reichstag_2.subtitle: Rumors of a President authorized unconstitutional decree...

content.content: It is rumored that by the end of last month, Chancellor von Papen secured Hindenburg's approval for two emergency decrees: one to dissolve the Reichstag, and another—blatantly unconstitutional—to postpone elections beyond the 60-day limit mandated by the Weimar Constitution. These decrees would allow Papen to govern unchallenged, free from the threat of parliamentary repeal or a vote of no confidence.

Papen has quickly become Hindenburg’s favorite, and the president—unwilling to part with him—has signed off on a decree that violates the constitution he swore to uphold. Former Chancellor Brüning, upon learning of this, has threatened Hindenburg with impeachment should he proceed, persuading himself that he'd deterred Papen from presenting the decree in the next session.

It's expected that General Schleicher would be the successor to Papen, however, being the Defense Minister and mastermind of the failed coup has severely damaged his standing as well. With new elections coming up soon, Hindenburg may choose to keep Papen in office, until a successor can be found with a new, more right-wing Reichstag.

papen_lausanne_conference_2.lausanne.title: At least we walked away with something.

content.content: Germany’s reparations burden has been slashed by 90%, with no payments due for another three years. This eases the strain on the national budget and gives the government new room to maneuver on monetary and fiscal policy.

Unfortunately for Papen, this does little to ease the near-universal hatred of his government. The far-right has denounced the treaty as a failure, outraged by his inability to secure any political or military concessions. Meanwhile, the republican parties and press have handed the credit to Brüning, who laid the groundwork for the conference in the first place. This development would've certainly been more impactful if Brüning had remained in office.

Papen’s tarnished reputation among the Western Allies has severely undermined Germany’s standing at the Geneva Disarmament Conference. With many now convinced that militarism has triumphed in Berlin, Schleicher’s efforts to negotiate military parity are likely to face steep resistance.

papen_lausanne_conference_2.title: Lausanne Conference Concludes
papen_lausanne_conference_2.subtitle: Germany's reparations payments are virtually abolished!

content.content: After weeks of difficult negotiations with the Western Allies, the German delegation at the Lausanne Conference has finally secured a result—though not the one it had hoped for. When talks hit a snag, Papen made a dramatic offer: a military alliance with France, sealed by an exchange of general staff officers. This only outraged the British and deepened French mistrust.

British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald tried to salvage the negotiations by proposing the repeal of disarmament clauses. But French Prime Minister Édouard Herriot rejected this outright—refusing any political discussions and treating Germany’s offer as an admission it could still pay. Backed into a corner, Papen’s delegation was left with no option but to offer a final payment of three billion marks—in exchange for nothing.

papen_lausanne_conference_1.lausanne.title: Anyhow, the German delegation is off to Switzerland.

content.content: At the opening session, our delegation demands the complete cancellation of reparations. This position has found sympathy from the British and the Americans. France’s new left-wing government has softened its stance as well—though they still insist that Germany enter a pact with the Western Allies, including provisions for military détente. Negotiations will continue in the coming weeks.

At the Lausanne Conference, the Allies will meet with German representatives to settle the reparations question once and for all. With the global economic crisis still raging, most now accept that Germany cannot resume payments once the current moratorium expires.

But with the reactionary nationalist Papen at the helm, Germany’s negotiating hand is weakened. The absence of the internationally respected Brüning, coupled with Papen’s reckless ambition to press for rearmament and a deletion of the 'war guilt' clause, threatens to derail the entire process.

options.title: The policy passes due to the emergency government; there is nothing we can do...

content.content: Chancellor Franz von Papen and his "Cabinet of Barons" are pushing forward an economic plan consisting of tax cuts for the very wealthy. This plan has the potential to lead to more economic growth, especially in comparison to Brüning's austerity program, but it also enriches the upper class and does nothing directly for the needy workers and unemployed.

options.title: Who will the candidates be now that Hindenburg is retiring?

content.content: President Hindenburg has decided not to run for re-election, citing his health problems and old age as the primary reasons. He feels that the current national situation doesn't warrant a reelection campaign.

This development could be either beneficial or detrimental to us. If we wanted to rally behind Hindenburg to oppose Hitler and the Nazis, the absence of a unifying, widely supported national figure—one capable of garnering support from both the moderate left and right—leaves us at a disadvantage. On the other hand, if we decide to run a candidate of our own, the lack of someone with Hindenburg's charisma could make it easier for us to secure a victory.
The absence of a candidate for the German middle and moderate right to rally behind creates a vacuum, which will likely be filled as other parties announce their candidates in the near future.

content.content: The State Court has ruled that the Prussian government did not fail in its duties, meaning the use of force against a state refusing to follow the constitution was unlawful and the application of the Reichsexekution was unjustified. However, the court did affirm that the government could still appoint a Reich Commissioner and temporarily assume control of Prussia due to a perceived threat to public safety and order.

content: Additionally, the court declared that the dismissal of the Prussian government was illegal and that Prussia’s representation in the Reichsrat must be restored. While acknowledging that the Prussian government remains legally intact, the judicial system’s reactionary nature meant that no practical change was enforced. The court’s ruling did not explicitly demand the reinstatement of the Prussian government, and the

government has ignored the decision. Holding the government accountable for this violation would require accusing President Hindenburg of breaching the law by signing the decree—an action the conservative judges find politically unacceptable.

Goerdeler, ever the conservative, sympathizes with these goals and steps down before Hindenburg can force the issue.

It is clear this is part of Papen’s wider plan for a "New State"—a centralized, anti-democratic regime ruled by aristocrats and the rich. The upcoming Prussian elections have now been postponed indefinitely.

content.content: President Hindenburg and Chancellor Schleicher have grown fed up with the political deadlock in Prussia and move to dismiss its government, replacing it with a Reichskommissar—likely one of their allies or another reactionary figure.

The move carries plausible justification, with Hindenburg citing Prussia's "ungovernable" state, brought on by repeated failures to form a stable government and escalating clashes between state forces and paramilitaries in these troubled times.

content.content: Our policy choices have greatly offended the reformist faction. Many of our most experienced leaders have resigned.

Now, many reformists have joined a splinter party, the *Sozial-Republikanische Partei Deutschlands* (Social-Republican Party of Germany), founded by former Reichsbanner leader Otto Hörsing, transforming it from a rump party into a viable competitor. They proclaim their desire to defend the Republic and the Constitution, and see us as having strayed from a pure Republican path. The SRPD has support from the workers and progressive middle class.

content.content: The pamphlet argues that a party tolerating homosexuality at its highest levels must seek to "poison the people and destroy its moral strength." It warns that this would lead to Germany’s decline, akin to the fall of ancient Rome, and claims that by keeping Röhm in power, the Nazis are complicit in "knowingly and intentionally furthering the seduction of German youths into becoming homosexual minions."

content.content: Meanwhile, the pamphlet’s publisher, Helmuth Klotz, has been brutally beaten by Nazi deputies inside the Reichstag building as an act of revenge—an event that has overshadowed the scandal itself.
This is an occasion to celebrate! Hopefully he Nazis will no longer be a threat to the Republic.

content.content: Groener, one of Brüning’s longest-standing and most loyal allies, is now out of the equation. Brüning, deeply loyal to him, was fully prepared to resign the chancellorship if Groener was forced out of the cabinet. However, unwilling to let Brüning risk his own position on his behalf, Groener chose to step down.

His resignation as Minister of Defense has dealt a severe blow to the Brüning cabinet, further diminishing its chances of surviving the deepening political crisis triggered by the fallout from the local elections. Among Hindenburg’s inner circle of advisors, no one had been more steadfast in supporting Brüning than Groener. His departure has severely weakened the chancellor’s standing with the Reich President, leaving him fully exposed to the machinations of Schleicher and his entourage.

With Groener gone, Schleicher is now free from external restraints to pursue his strategy of taming the Nazis, answerable only to Hindenburg. Sensing that Brüning has been fatally weakened, the Nazis have intensified their attacks on his government, seeking to bring it down once and for all.

content.content: Schleicher, once reviled by the public, is now hailed as Germany’s savior. Through his public works campaign and ruthlessly pragmatic ideology, he has managed to win support from across the political spectrum. But a key question remains: where can these grateful voters turn to express their support for the chancellor?

schleicher_cabinet_1.subtitle: A Commissioner for Employment is established for planned public works...

content.content: Chancellor Schleicher has unveiled his new cabinet—retaining all but two of Papen’s ministers. His top priority, he claims, is putting people back to work. To that end, he has appointed Günther Gereke, President of the Rural Municipal Congress and a reformist economic theorist, as Reichskommissar for Employment, with a full seat in the cabinet.

For now, Schleicher is enjoying a political honeymoon. The relief at Papen’s fall has been widespread, and his public disavowal of any plans to alter the constitution has calmed both the national mood and the republicans who had bitterly opposed his predecessor.

content: The Christian trade unions and their affiliated parties have adopted a conciliatory stance, while the ADGB and
leaderships, viewing Schleicher as the lesser evil, have responded positively to his public works proposals.

content.content: But the real issue isn’t popular unrest—it’s whether Schleicher can survive the no-confidence vote looming in the Reichstag later this week.

However, their entry into government has strained our relations, as they had previously stood in united opposition with us.

The main obstacle, however, is the Center Party’s deep reservations about sharing a cabinet with the Nazis. To overcome this, Schleicher and the
have signaled their readiness to fast-track a Reichskonkordat with the Vatican—an offer that Kaas, a longtime advocate of such, finds difficult to refuse.

content.content: Having achieved his lifelong goal, Kaas sees little reason to remain as leader of the Center Party—a position he had long described as a burden and expressed displeasure with. As a result, a new leadership race is set to take place within the party, with Schleicher able to influence the outcome through his connections with Kaas and the Christian Trade Unions.
The candidate backed by the Christian unions and those advocating for a more interconfessional Center Party rallies around Stegerwald.

content: , has rejoined the party and is Schleicher’s preferred candidate. Bracht is a true believer in Schleicher's vision for a new Germany—one less entangled in parliamentarianism—and aligns with the Center's right wing, though not as far right as Papen. However, due to his lack of influence within the party and limited prior experience, having served only as Mayor of Essen for eight years, it is Schleicher's backing that remains the key to elevating him to leadership.

We know all of this is nonsense, but Schleicher has slowly taken steps toward the Gleichschaltung (synchronization) of his regime, having recently established the "Ministry of National Guidance" in the decree in which he banned the

content.content: For now, the organization remains confined to Prussia, but its presence is felt everywhere. Local party members whisper that their phones are tapped, and troublesome politicians vanish—never to be seen again. With the police now firmly under government control, they decide which crimes to overlook and coordinate raids hand-in-hand with the Reichswehr.
Yet, their reach still depends on the willingness of people to betray their comrades by reporting them to the police.

Two men of a fading generation are nearing their end.

content.content: Unbeknownst to the public, Schleicher has been suffering from pernicious anemia for several years. As early as 1930, his family doctor warned him that, given the stress and heavy responsibilities of his career, he likely had no more than six years to live. Now, with the added strain of the chancellorship, those who interact with him have begun to notice his steady decline into lethargy. He may only have a few months left.

In a public announcement, Schleicher announces his resignation, stating that he will soon handpick a successor to be appointed by Hindenburg. He never truly enjoyed the role, and in recent months has quietly delegated his duties to trusted allies in the Reichswehr, grooming them to take his place.
The question now: who will carry forward Schleicher's legacy?

title: Carl Friedrich Goerdeler - <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
schleicher_cabinet_19.goerdeler.subtitle: Former nationalist mayor of Leipzig. Strong conservative.

content: Goerdeler, an outspoken conservative on the German Right, with personal authoritarian and monarchist leanings, represents Schleicher’s signal of a return to partisan rule in essence. Despite breaking with his former party to join the <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
, his appointment is seen by workers and republicans as little different from naming a

content.content: Yet, the fact that he is not a military figure like Schleicher or his circle has brought some measure of relief. Though a long-time opponent of Alfred Hugenberg and his faction, Goerdeler remains a conservative at heart and is expected to continue the dismantling of the despised Weimar order.

But Goerdeler is no Schleicher. He lacks the vast network of political ties that his patron carefully cultivated across German society, and Schleicher’s personal popularity has failed to pass to his chosen successor. Moreover, Goerdeler is known for his hardline fiscal conservatism and anti-social stance, having once called for the abolition of unemployment insurance during the Papen era.
Perhaps the house of cards Schleicher so carefully built is already beginning to wobble.

content: The German people had only briefly united behind their so-called savior, General Kurt von Schleicher. Now, with a return to political normalcy looming, there is no place for an incoherent vehicle like the <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
to rally the nation behind lofty abstractions like "non-partisanship" and the Volksgemeinschaft.

content.content: With Schleicher nearing the end—both politically and personally—he is in no position to stop the unraveling of his own creation. Perhaps this will be remembered as his greatest blunder: that everything he built ends in anticlimax. Yet the Weimar system has already been gutted over the past few years.

The Blocparteis are freed, and the bulk of the organization — those not drawn from their ranks — has splintered off in different directions. The right-wing, more nationalist section has salvaged the party's national structures and will continue on by merging into the
The more left-leaning—and quite frankly, eccentric—elements of the movement have formed a new Old Social Democratic Party (

content.content: We cannot expect much cooperation from this group. Yet, oddly enough, the two splinter factions have found common ground—agreeing to tolerate, and even participate in, the Treviranus cabinet.

Although not directly related to recent negotiations, a scandal was revealed during a session of the Reichstag’s budget committee: a Center Party member leveled sweeping accusations of fraud against beneficiaries of the Eastern Aid program. Meant to rescue bankrupt estates, the funds were allegedly used instead for racehorses, luxury cars, and lavish holidays—at a time when millions of Germans were living in poverty.

content: President Hindenburg himself has been implicated. His

estate—a gift from right-wing industrialists and the RLB in 1927—was transferred into his son Oskar’s name to avoid taxes. Though not legally contestable, the revelation that many of Hindenburg’s close friends also benefited has deeply unsettled the President, who is now inundated with complaints from his old allies.

content.content: Given Schleicher’s reputation for shadowy political maneuvering, and the fact that these revelations surfaced just a day after his break with the RLB, many suspect that he orchestrated the leak as an act of revenge.

schleicher_cabinet_2.title: Schleicher and the Agrarians
schleicher_cabinet_2.subtitle: The RLB is disappointed in Schleicher's agricultural policy.

content.content: Schleicher’s economic and agricultural ministers remain locked in a bitter struggle over tariffs—part of the broader conflict between industrialists and agrarians. Schleicher has refused to take a side, maintaining a façade of unity for the public. However, his failure to uphold a promise to continue Papen’s protectionist policies—meant to shield German farm products from cheap foreign imports—has led the increasingly right-wing National Rural League (RLB) to turn against him.

President Hindenburg, like many conservative Germans of his generation, viewed agriculture as the bedrock of national life—a source of tradition and moral strength. It was he who, of his own accord, summoned the economic and agricultural ministers, along with Schleicher, to a meeting with the RLB. The cabinet temporarily mollified the situation by promising future action.

content: Yet Hindenburg and the RLB remained dissatisfied, particularly over the government’s failure to renew a decree shielding bankrupt farmers from foreclosure. In truth, however, the RLB had long since become a political instrument of the

, more interested in toppling Schleicher than securing concessions. Despite the earlier agreement, they publicly attacked the chancellor—prompting an angry Schleicher to break off further talks. Hindenburg, under the influence of his

content.content: Eventually, Schleicher relented and agreed to issue a new measure protecting bankrupt farmers from foreclosure.

Instead, he recommends the appointment of rising star and Volkskonservativ leader Gottfried Treviranus. With deep ties to German industry, the Right, and a pseudo-republican veneer, Treviranus is a candidate aimed at stabilizing Germany’s worsening crisis.

content: Much like Papen’s dismissal in favor of Schleicher, the political class breathes yet another sigh of relief. Even within the <span style="color: #c00000;">

content.content: With his faith in the Reichswehr shattered, he has turned back to his old allies among the nationalists. And with the bar set so low, perhaps this is a blessing to us. Though they remain our enemies, as they were in the days of normalcy, whoever Hindenburg selects now is likely to be preferable to Schleicher’s continued hold on office.

Despite the clear advantages of the third option, Schleicher rejects it. He hints that even if the Reichstag cannot oust him directly, a hostile majority could still repeal his emergency decrees—rendering his position untenable. True to Prussian military tradition, which favors offense over defense and prizes personal courage in the face of adversity, Schleicher may find it too humiliating to swallow his pride and retreat from his earlier threats to dissolve the Reichstag.

Nevertheless, he decides to ask the President for authorization to dissolve the Reichstag and postpone new elections—despite Oskar likely having convinced his father to oppose this course weeks ago. His position is weakened by the fact that he previously brought down Papen, in front of the very cabinet members he retains today, by claiming the Reichswehr could not handle the outrage such a blatantly unconstitutional move would provoke.

Schleicher now argues that circumstances have changed. His outreach to the labor unions, he claims, has neutralized the risk of civil war, and his economic plan will soon reduce tensions. As Defense Minister, he also asserts that he has addressed the Reichswehr’s deficiencies—it is now better prepared, with greatly expanded stocks of tear gas and streetfighting gear.
Schleicher lays out four scenarios before the President:
3. His own cabinet continuing under presidential emergency powers—his recommendation.
4. A disastrous cabinet led by Papen and Hugenberg—likely to provoke civil war.
He does not request a postponement of elections this time—only a commitment from Hindenburg to dissolve the chamber upon reconvening.
He is denied. Hindenburg acknowledges Schleicher’s efforts to win over the Nazis, but with that effort having failed, the President declares it time to explore “another possibility.”

content.content: The nation needs a break from more polarizing elections. Let the chancellor govern.

Schleicher was never a true believer in converting his cabinet into a parliamentary one, and he undercut his own threat to call new elections by suggesting that no one would object if they were delayed beyond the constitutionally mandated 60 days. In reality, nothing could be further from the truth.

Even so, Schleicher now seeks to secure a decree—similar to the one he once offered Papen but which was never enacted, as the Reichstag president simply ignored him. Should Hindenburg refuse to issue such a decree, it won’t signal a renewed commitment to constitutional norms. Rather, it would confirm the scope of the conspiracy against Schleicher—one that now includes the President himself.

The plan is approved by the chancellor and signed by Hindenburg without objection. With Schleicher fulfilling a widely popular promise, and the republican parties beginning to soften their stance on the government, it seems that Schleicher may be here to stay.

content.content: Presumably aiming to win over the unions' affiliated parties—the Center Party and the SPD—and to bolster public confidence in his leadership at the grassroots level, Schleicher has enacted a new decree.

An eight-hour workday is now mandated across most industries, intended to "spread out" employment among more workers. The means test for unemployment insurance has been abolished, and welfare funding has been increased to offset years of austerity.

The Social General has lived up to his nickname. Yet, cynically, the cost is clear—Schleicher now wields significant leverage over the unions, and many workers are beginning to shift their loyalty toward the chancellor, who delivers results, rather than the opposition parties. His image as a strongman, standing above the old parties, is slowly conditioning the workers to accept a more authoritarian system.

members, who rise through bribes, patronage, and backroom deals. Corruption is endemic. Elections are stage-managed, dominated by fraud and manipulation.
is never formally banned and endures as a powerless "loyal opposition," unable to influence national policy. Though tolerated, they face constant harassment and suppression by the ruling regime.

content.content: Despite the regime’s authoritarianism, social discontent remains subdued. A Wirtschaftswunder—an economic miracle—emerges as the Great Depression fades. In 1935, Germany secures equality in armaments at Geneva and begins agitating for the return of the Polish Corridor separating East Prussia from the Reich.

In 1942, a "special military operation" is launched to seize Danzig. Poland refuses to cede territory, and with backing from France and a hesitant Britain, enters a state of war. A puppet regime is installed in occupied territories. A limited French offensive into the Saar fails, and the Western Allies remain at war only on paper.

Sensing German isolation, the Soviet Union invades eastern Poland, citing abuses against native Belarusians and Ukrainians under military occupation. A new German–Soviet war erupts. Defense Minister Hammerstein cultivates ties with the "Little Entente"—states facing their own Soviet-backed revolutionary threats. An unofficial Mitteleuropa bloc emerges, with Germany at its core, squeezed between a Western capitalist bloc and the Eastern state-socialist order.

In 1946, the war ends in stalemate. Poland is partitioned at the Vistula River. Romania and Bulgaria fall under Communist control. Western Europe grows closer to the United States, and a tripolar global order takes shape.

By the late 1960s, economic stagnation and renewed domestic unrest—driven by the Red Army Faction and neo-Nazi agitation—force Chancellor Kurt Georg Kiesinger to begin relaxing the dictatorship. The corporatist house of cards that had maintained the regime's stability for decades begins to crumble as independent unions discreetly form. However, Germany remains far from a free and democratic country, the Reichswehr maintains constant watch over politics, exercising real control behind the scenes.

content.content: The German Republic, called by some of our detractors as the "Weimar Republic", is a parliamentary republic with a somewhat weak president and a strong parliament, called the Reichstag. The Reichstag is responsible for governing, while the President has a largely ceremonial role but also has some important governing responsibilities.

The Reichstag is elected based on a proportional representation system, giving parties seats roughly proportional to their vote share in each electoral district. The Reichstag then elects the Chancellor and the cabinet by a majority vote, who are responsible for government. A majority vote-of-no-confidence can remove the current government.

The President is elected by a national direct vote, in two rounds. The second round is used if the first round does not result in a majority for one candidate; the candidate who receives a plurality in the second round becomes president (there is no obligation for weaker candidates to drop out). The role of the president is mostly to represent Germany, but he also has some crucial governing powers. The president and chancellor can together use emergency decrees to govern, bypassing the Reichstag. The president can also appoint or remove a chancellor when a parliamentary majority is unable to be established, and can thus influence the formation of a government.
Germany is divided into a number of states, each of which have their own governments with some responsibilities. By far the largest and most important state is Prussia.

content.content: Expectedly, the Lautenbach Plan has failed due to strong opposition from those who adhere to fiscal orthodoxy, which holds that deflation, despite its pain, is healthy because it weeds out inefficient producers. This contrasts with the Keynesian belief that a destructive second phase occurs, where economic recovery becomes possible but fails because of a collapse in investor confidence.

Reichsbank President Hans Luther, who personally sympathizes with increasing the money supply and expanding credit, has shelved the idea. The conference only reached two unanimous conclusions: the German people's fear of inflation made it impossible to announce any dramatic program to expand the money supply, meaning the government would have to act secretly if it ever decided to implement Lautenbach's plan, and the government must continue its campaign to lower wages bound by long-term collective labor contracts and prices set by cartel agreements.

However, Luther has made concessions to the Keynesians, quietly expanding the money supply and increasing credit availability, even abandoning the rule that 40% of money in circulation must be covered by gold and foreign exchange. Furthermore, generous financing of exports to the Soviet Union has helped counteract the effects of the withdrawal of foreign credits on both the money supply and the job market.

content.content: Act for the Protection of the Economy and Finance

To eliminate the growing deficit in the national budget, Brüning has introduced an act that enforces sweeping government spending cuts while implementing a special “crisis tax” and raising various other taxes. To justify the hardships imposed on German society, Brüning coupled its promulgation with a public appeal, urging Germany’s international creditors to acknowledge the sacrifices demanded of the German people by providing relief from the nation’s “intolerable” reparations burden.

content.content: It has been thirteen years since the adoption of the Weimar Constitution in 1919—a date still marked as a public holiday in its commemoration.

However, Papen has chosen this occasion to unveil his plan for a so-called “New State”: an authoritarian constitution that would merge the offices of chancellor and Prussian minister president, free the chancellor from reliance on Reichstag confidence, and establish an aristocratic upper house of parliament appointed by the president. In practice, this would transform Germany into a dictatorship run by elites.

content: The Reichstag has reconvened for the first time since the election, with a significantly larger contingent of <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

members now present. The immediate issue at hand is the election of the President of the Reichstag. While the position has traditionally been a procedural one, it has taken on heightened importance under Papen's presidential government, given the President's authority to influence the agenda and adjourn sessions.
By long-standing custom, the role is granted to the largest parliamentary delegation. That delegation isn't the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
, but the Center Party backing them nonetheless is a key part of negotiations between the two parties. Without such backing, it is likely that our candidate, Paul Löbe, would be elected once again.
have secured unanimous approval for a change in the order of business to allow an immediate vote on a motion of no confidence against Papen, and not even the
was willing to lift a finger to prevent this.

With no objection, the vote was to begin just as Chancellor von Papen has arrived inside the Reichstag to present his emergency decree to the chamber, disrupting his plans to present both decrees at once. He had placed the folder on Reichstag President
's desk, and demanded him to read it to the floor. However,
has trick up his sleeve: he could pretend he didn't see it and proceed with the no confidence motion anyway.
In the end, Papen is defeated by a humiliating margin with
% of the Reichstag voting against him, only supported by the

presidential_election_1932_hindenburg.subtitle: The President is to announce whether or not he will run again.

content: President Hindenburg has expressed his reluctance to run for re-election. At 84 years old, he prefers to spend his remaining years in retirement free from the burdens of his high office. While he has been open to serving longer if his term were extended by the Reichstag, the failure of those efforts, combined with his unwillingness to endure a grueling presidential campaign, has caused concern, particularly for Kurt von Schleicher
, on whom he depends to enact his decrees
Heinrich Sahm, the Mayor of Berlin, has formed a re-election committee to persuade Hindenburg to run again. This effort has included the collection of over

million signatures and appeals from a wide array of figures and political parties across German society, including Artur Mahraun of the Young German Order, and controversial former Defense Ministers Otto Gessler and Gustav Noske.

Impressed by the public support, Hindenburg is reconsidering his decision but insists that his candidacy must be backed by the German Right and veteran organizations rather than the German Left and Center.

content.content: The invitation for a direct meeting between Theodor Leipart, leader of the ADGB, and von Schleicher is declined. Instead, a larger meeting is held, including Papen, his Interior Minister, and the ADGB’s co-chairs.

content: At the meeting, the union leaders confront Schleicher over alleged secret agreements with the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
, prompting both Schleicher and Papen to strike a more conciliatory tone in response to union complaints about unfair government treatment. Schleicher denies any such deals with the
, insisting that the government's highest priority is reducing unemployment. Papen also requests the unions to use their influence to persuade the
to give the government time to deliver results.

content.content: By the end of the meeting, the three unionists are left impressed by Schleicher, who hints at possible concessions to a “patriotic labor movement.” A line of communication between the ADGB and the government remains open—much to Wels’s frustration, as he aims to maintain a united front against the regime.

The topic of the conference was about possible joint action between the Reichswehr and the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
