content.content: Who are we to abandon committed republicans willing to stand with us? They may prove a useful ally against Schleicher’s regime, even if they’re only expected to draw about a single percent of the vote in the next election.

content: Schleicher now wields extensive influence over the <span style="color: #c00000;">

, and even greater sway within our affiliated trade union, the ADGB. Exploiting this grip—alongside a relentless psychological campaign among the rank-and-file and open intimidation by the Reichswehr militia, which threatens action if no decision is made before the deadline—Schleicher forces their submission to the German Labor Front—soon to be integrated.
The new ADGB chairmen waste no time: they denounce all ties to political parties and pledge loyalty to nothing but the nation. Marxist doctrine is stamped out, and the radical

content.content: The fall of the ADGB marks the beginning of the end. If even the workers no longer stand with us—what power do we really have left?

options.title: The German National Unity Front welcomes its new members.

content: , once buoyed by their early popularity as one of the few parties to unconditionally back Papen, have since soured their relations with the chancellery. Hugenberg's demand for full control over the agricultural and economic ministries has strained ties, and his uncompromising opposition to Schleicher has sparked discontent within the
—a party once built entirely from his loyalists.

content.content: Many of his former allies are now bewildered that Hugenberg would turn against a fellow reactionary, especially one who ostensibly shares his vision of steering Germany toward authoritarian rule.

With Hugenberg’s personal fortune—once sustained by his media empire—running dry, and industrial backers remaining firmly opposed to his leadership, frustrated members and former confidants are abandoning ship. They now flock to the German National Unity Front, preferring to back Schleicher directly without Hugenberg standing in their way.

content.content: The unification of the labor unions has complicated Schleicher's efforts to divide and conquer, depriving him of the option to play the more moderate unions against the ADGB. We have also agreed to coordinate unified action in response to any offensive measures his government may attempt in the coming months.

schleicher_2.wait.title: Persuade the Reichsbanner to remain non-committal for now, at least until the next election.

content: We have secured a commitment from the Reichsbanner leadership not to make any official decision regarding participation in the
before the upcoming elections—a compromise between the party factions. However, some local members may still choose to enroll in the training programs on their own initiative.
The Interior Ministry returns to Schleicher loyalist Franz Bracht, while Hjalmar Schacht retains his position as Economic Minister. Nazis who have chosen to join the
are generously rewarded with government positions.

title: The <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
Breaks with Schleicher!
schleicher_22.subtitle: Strasser realizes he has fallen into Schleicher’s trap.

options.title: Out of funds, out of followers, out of luck.

content.content: Now, a bitter realization dawns on Strasser and his top Nazi lieutenants: they’ve been used. Schleicher has no intention of letting them control anything beyond the Interior Ministry. Worse, their party has been bleeding support in local elections, punished for failing to deliver on its grand promises.

content: After all, it’s Schleicher the people thank for their jobs—not the <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
, whose fights with the Bolsheviks do little to put food on the table for their electoral base. The formation of the
has only deepened the wound, as many of their former voters flock to this new pole of order and stability.

schleicher_5.subtitle: We must either confirm or deny a supposed deal between the ADGB and the chancellor.

content: With Theodor Leipart’s announcement that he would support a Schleicher cabinet if Papen were the only alternative, numerous leaks have surfaced to the public—much to the annoyance of those in the <span style="color: #c00000;">
. Many workers still view Schleicher as merely a continuation of the despised Papen cabinet, and it remains in our electoral interest to uphold total opposition to him.

Meanwhile, the ADGB has sought to shape Schleicher’s proposed public works program and fears that a parliamentary ousting would pave the way for Papen’s return. The specifics of our negotiations have been exaggerated—and in many cases, outright misreported—creating a serious public relations crisis among the <span style="color: #c00000;">

content.content: What should our stance be moving forward?

title: The <span style="color: #c00000;">
Slips Away
schleicher_21.subtitle: We handed Schleicher too much influence over us.

content.content: Low-ranking party members loyal to Schleicher have steadily climbed the ranks, until a new executive committee finally replaces the old guard that had served the party since the founding of the republic.

At its head now stand Schleicher’s yes-men—figures like the notorious former Defense Minister Gustav Noske and Lothar Erdmann, a nationalist voice within the ADGB, fiercely hostile to the Treaty of Versailles and far closer to Schleicher’s ideology than the mere pragmatism of Braun or Leipart.
The German National Unity Front welcomes its new member.
Nothing ultimately comes of the meeting. However, Braun becomes the first major political figure outside the unions to openly signal willingness to strike a deal with the chancellor.

schleicher_6.title: Braun Meets With Schleicher
schleicher_6.subtitle: An unauthorized meeting, but perhaps a welcome one?

content: Otto Braun, former Minister-President of Prussia and leader of our reformist wing, has—without informing the <span style="color: #c00000;">

leadership—met privately with Chancellor von Schleicher. Braun proposed cooperation, on the condition that Schleicher relinquish federal control over Prussia and restore him to office with full authority, including the power to dissolve the Landtag. Braun suggested that, together, they could rule by decree and wage a determined campaign against the Nazis.

Schleicher, however, was unenthusiastic. Having led the Prussian coup himself, he is reluctant to undo the federal consolidation of power. More importantly, unlike Braun, he is not committed to weakening the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
; he still views them as a potential source of support for his cabinet—admiring the
’s fanatical discipline as traits to be co-opted into the state.

schleicher_4.nay.title: We need the sharpest opposition to the new Schleicher cabinet. Order the ADGB and Reichsbanner to boycott the Institute for Youth Fitness.

content.content: Our explicit rejection of Reichsbanner participation in the program has caused discontent within both the ADGB and the Reichsbanner, who have nonetheless reluctantly yielded to the party leadership’s decision.
As a socialist party, we cannot lend our support to what is, in essence, a thinly veiled rearmament scheme.

schleicher_4.title: Schleicher and the Reichsbanner
subtitle: It's time to decide our stance on the

content.content: Weeks ago, Schleicher reached out to the socialist youth organizations and the Reichsbanner to gauge their interest in participating in the Reich Institute to Promote Youth Fitness. The program, led by retired Reichswehr officers, aims to teach "military sports" to young workers.
We've taken a non-committal stance, putting off the issue until after the elections, and now, the General himself is chancellor.
We can either build goodwill and strengthen the Reichsbanner through our participation, or maintain our total opposition against the presidential cabinets and boycott it.

The Social Patriots advocate full support for Schleicher’s chancellorship and his rearmament program, believing that only through strength can Germany break free from the chains of Versailles and reclaim its rightful lands.

content: Schleicher is displeased with our moves to curb the influence of his loyalists within the <span style="color: #c00000;">
— but for now, this ideology remains far from our party’s leadership. For now.

subtitle: A new faction takes shape within the <span style="color: #c00000;">

options.title: Who said patriotism and socialism aren't compatible?
There's no war but the class war.

content.content: A newer faction of young and old socialists, led by ADGB unionist Lothar Erdmann, is rallying under the banner of "Social Patriotism." This group calls for a renewed bond between the workers, socialism, and the nation. Erdmann is the architect of the ADGB's nationalist shift in recent years, including its sharpened rhetoric against the Treaty of Versailles.
This is plainly Schleicher’s handiwork—yet this emerging faction now holds real sway within our party, given the Chancellor’s grip on our more "patriotic" and loosely Marxist trade unions.

content: We have publicly broken with Schleicher, presenting the frankly thin evidence to the public—including a shady 3-million Reichsmark donation to the <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
Schleicher dismisses it as simple politics, but many voters aren’t convinced. They’re rallying behind us as
democratic choice, now alert to democratic backsliding.

content: Schleicher has made it clear he won’t establish a military dictatorship—after all, how could the Western Allies trust us if he can’t even maintain the façade of democracy? But that won’t stop him from meddling in our democratic processes, or so our informants claim. We have proof that Schleicher has funneled significant state funds to the
Maybe Schleicher hasn’t done anything at all, and this is just the paranoia of the anti-Schleicher factions within the <span style="color: #c00000;">
Either way, it’s given fresh ammunition to the <span style="color: #c00000;">

schleicher_cabinet_11.bracht.unavailableSubtitle: The Center Party is still rooted in republicanism.

content.content: Undoubtedly thanks to Schleicher's meddling, Franz Bracht has been elected chairman of the Center Party. With Kaas’s endorsement and Schleicher's ability to "persuade" key party members to switch their votes, Bracht narrowly defeats Stegerwald and his more republican support base.

The internal reaction has been surprisingly muted. Perhaps the Center Party’s gradual shift to the right has made a reactionary like Bracht finally acceptable—or perhaps other forces are quietly at work.

schleicher_cabinet_12.do_nothing.title: We should be grateful that nothing happened to us!

content: It must suck for those <span style="color: #700000;">

content.content: They should’ve simply not burned down the Reichstag. What were they thinking—are they stupid? Cynically, we might even benefit from this. As the only legal Marxist party left standing, we could capture the votes that have nowhere else to go.
We have leverage, and we should use it to extract concessions. No one wants civil war.

We have decided to cooperate with the government by preemptively dissolving the organization and turning over weapons before the ban is to take place. A notable amount of socialists have decided to fight on however, but without numbers or weapons, this ad-hoc group is destined for failure.
Schleicher hasn't expressed the gratitude for our cooperation like we hoped. Perhaps we outlived our usefulness to him.

schleicher_cabinet_16.title: The Reichsbanner Is Banned!
schleicher_cabinet_16.subtitle: Our so-called "revolutionary militia" is now officially outlawed nationwide.

content: Following months of state repression, the hollowed-out remnants of the Reichsbanner are officially banned. With the more moderate fighters having retired or been absorbed into the state’s militias, only die-hard socialists remain in the self-defense organization. This has given Schleicher the pretext to brand the
and the Reichsbanner as jointly conspiring toward revolutionary overthrow—and to extend the ban to both.

content.content: If this ban goes through, we will be left defenseless against state oppression. Many in the party urge us to resist, while others claim that the era of paramilitaries is over and argue for preemptive disarmament to placate Schleicher.

title: Ferdinand von Bredow - <span style="color: #BFC8CC;">
schleicher_cabinet_19.bredow.subtitle: Deputy Defense Minister. Ideology suspected to be similar to Schleicher's.

content.content: Presenting himself as a continuation of Schleicher and as another non-partisan military man, von Bredow has won his close friend Schleicher's favor. Although former chancellor Schleicher is officially retired, he still pulls many strings behind the scenes, unwilling to give up that scheming of his.

However, von Bredow is certainly no Schleicher, he possesses no vast network of political connections throughout all walks of life, and Schleicher's personal popularity has largely failed to transfer over to his hand picked successor.
Perhaps the house of cards Schleicher has carefully built will come tumbling down?

With his resignation announced last week, speculation over who will succeed the monumental leader now dominates the minds of citizens across the nation. Some believe he is prepared to pass power to a civilian, while others expect another military man to take the helm. In the end, it hardly matters—Germany has been changed forever.

Also predicting that a new election wouldn't alter the Reichstag in his favor much, he also asks for a decree postponing the planned election.

Hindenburg remains unresponsive. His personal estrangement from Schleicher is already far advanced, and there have been little personal contact between the two men for a majority of Schleicher's term. Schleicher advocating for the same course of action that he himself opposed when it was advocated by Papen.

In the end, Hindenburg is only willing to provide a dissolution decree, but then he refuses to provide it to Schleicher as of right now. But to the public, Schleicher's hold on the chancellorship remains firm.
Schleicher returns to his waiting ministers and relays the outcome. An announcement of his resignation—prepared weeks in advance—is released to the press.

content.content: The Reichsbank, long known for its strict fiscal conservatism and obsessive anti-inflation stance, had already slashed Schleicher's initial public works decree by 15%. So, it was no surprise when news of even greater government spending met with their disapproval.

However, the endorsement of the campaign by Hjalmar Schacht—a respected banker and recently retired Reichsbank President credited with ending hyperinflation—has done much to calm the business community. Under government pressure, the Reichsbank is ultimately coerced into backing the plan, though not without forcing another 20% cut in funding.

content: Papen, eager to return to power and thirsting for revenge against his former ally and ouster Schleicher, has been working behind the scenes to arrange a meeting with
. With the help of intermediaries—and ultimately a banker sympathetic to the Nazis—he finally secured an audience with the man himself.

The two met at the banker’s home, where they spent much of the time airing old grievances. Nevertheless, Papen made a concerted effort to court the Nazi leader. He insisted that it was Schleicher, not he, who had blocked

’s path to the chancellorship. He also revealed that President Hindenburg had yet to issue Schleicher a decree to dissolve the Reichstag—evidence, he claimed, of the president’s deep reservations about him. Papen emphasized that the true nature of the Hindenburg-Schleicher relationship was far more strained than the public believed, and he asserted that he himself still wielded considerable influence over the old man. His hatred for Schleicher was unmistakable throughout.

content.content: By the end of the meeting, the two had reached a mutual understanding: they would work together to oust Schleicher and replace his government with a presidential cabinet based on a coalition between the Nazis and the reactionary right, with the goal of crushing the leftist parties once and for all.

content: However, the question of who should lead this new government remained unresolved. Papen argued that Hindenburg’s well-known opposition to appointing
should make him the more viable candidate, offering to give the Nazis control over the Interior and Defense Ministries as compensation.
flatly rejected this, still insisting that his mass movement had earned the right to the chancellorship.

content.content: The meeting concluded with a promise to continue discussions, though no future date was set.

ending_slides.weimar_win.title: The Weimar Republic Limps Forward
ending_slides.weimar_win.subtitle: Ending 2

content: Following the scarring experience of the Nazi movement’s rapid rise and implosion, the flaws of the Weimar system became impossible to ignore. But in the end, the fascists and communists who once battled in the streets now stand together in soup lines. Though a number of neo-Nazi movements would emerge after
’s mask of sanity slipped, the ideology itself remains irrevocably discredited.

No war as destructive as the Great War would come again. Slowly, Germany and the Western Allies began to rebuild relations, choosing to forget and forgive. Fascism never takes root as a dominant force, and the primary threat to European democracy becomes the resurgent Soviet Union. The Spanish Civil War ends in 1936 with a Republican victory.

content.content: In 1939, Austria's Austrofascist regime collapses under popular revolt.

content.content: Timeline of the SPD and the Republic (until 1928)

content: : The SPD is formed as a merger of the General German Workers' Association, founded by Ferdinand Lassalle, and the Social Democratic Workers' Party of Germany, led by Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel. Eventually, the SPD grows to become the largest party in the German Empire.
: The Great War begins. The SPD votes in favor of war credits, with substantial internal dissent. This begins a policy of
, a general peace between all political parties and trade unions.
: The USPD, a left-wing anti-war split from the SPD, is formed.

: Following defeats in the war and uprisings by soldiers, sailors, and workers, SPD leader Philip Scheidemann proclaims the German Republic, and Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates from his throne. An armistice is declared, ending the Great War. Conflict between center-left social democrats and far-left radicals erupts in the streets of Berlin and elsewhere.

: The Spartacist Uprising, in which communist workers attempt to seize control of government, is launched. The uprising is defeated by the Social Democratic government, now led by President Friedrich Ebert and Chancellor Philipp Scheidemann, with the support of the far-right Freikorps militas. The two key leaders of the uprising, Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, are murdered by the Freikorps. The Treaty of Versailles is signed under great protest from all political factions in Germany, officially ending the Great War. The Weimar Constitution is signed. The first "Weimar Coalition" government is formed, led by the SPD, DDP, and Center (Z) parties.

: The Kapp Putsch, an attempt by reactionary actors within the military to take power, is launched, and is defeated by the workers with a general strike. This is followed by left-wing uprisings in the Ruhr, which are defeated by the Reichswehr and Freikorps. The Weimar Coalition is defeated in the elections, with the right and far left increasing in vote share. Elected governments in this period are very unstable, often only lasting a matter of months. There is a split in the USPD, with the majority faction joining with the KPD and the Soviet Union's Communist International (Comintern) alliance.
: Communist uprisings in Saxony and Hamburg are defeated. Matthias Erzberger, the Center Party leader who signed the Versailles Treaty, is assassinated.
: The Treaty of Rapallo is signed, which normalized relations with the Soviet Union. Walther Rathenau, the DDP Foreign Minister, is assassinated. The SPD reunites with most of the remaining USPD.

: Hyperinflation begins, largely due to the economic policy of "passive resistance" against the French occupation of the Ruhr and the Versailles reparations. The currency is rapidly devalued as prices for necessities rise to billions of Reichsmarks. The government launches a Reichsexekution against Saxony, which was led by a joint SPD-KPD government. The Nazi "Beer Hall Putsch" is launched in Munich, and fails, with the arrest of Hitler. Eventually, new policies manage to stabilize the currency, and the French occupation ends.

: Parliamentary elections are held in May and December, the latter leading to the bourgeois-right governments that last until 1928. Hitler is released from prison. The Dawes Plan for the repayment of the Versailles reparations is negotiated, which reduces payments and increases economic growth. Germany begins to enter a period of relative stability, with the end of the hyperinflation crisis.

: President Friedrich Ebert dies, and new presidential elections are held, leading to the narrow election of Paul von Hindenburg in the second round. Hindenburg is a war hero and a right-wing reactionary. The SPD adopts the Heidelberg Program as its party platform. The Locarno Treaties are signed, which confirmed Germany's post-war western borders.
: A referendum on the expropriation of the princes, supported by the SPD and KPD, fails.

game_over.war_against_hitler.title: Adolf Hitler is in power, but we are fighting to stop him.

content.content: Adolf Hitler has taken power in Germany. However, we have rallied the democratic forces of the country against him, and are fighting back. The outcome of this war is uncertain.
Hindenburg keeps sacking me! How do I prevent it?

It's hard to prevent him from sacking you if you plan to stay in office for the full four years, but pausing reparations (by not exposing rearmament), keeping the Reichswehr loyal, maintaining a budget surplus, keeping a high pro republic support, a low coalition dissent, avoiding land reform, and keeping unemployment and NSDAP poll numbers low, all help. Remember, him sacking you is not the end of the world, and being free from the burden of government could be a blessing in disguise. Sometimes you have to accept it.

A main problem with newer players is that, they overestimate the negative effects of not completing government burden. It is not the end of the world if you miss a goal or two or three, some sacrifices are needed if you need to garner the budget for an economic plan. That said, you also can't afford to completely ignore the Labor Ministry; repeated failures there will significantly increase internal dissent.
How do I impact a party's ideologies and get certain paths? Is it RNG?

content: Nothing in Dynamic relies on RNG, aside from card draws. The Support for the Republic value plays a crucial role in determining party congress outcomes, particularly within the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">

. The liberal parties, on the other hand, are primarily influenced by governmental actions—moving toward economic democracy and left-wing policies will push them rightward, while maintaining good relations and avoiding major socialist policies will bring them closer. Relations also matter significantly, making the negotiation skills of Müller and Braun highly valuable.

content.content: What happened to the WTB Plan?

Woytinsky only came up with the plan in late 1931 after the Banking Crisis, so to represent this, you need to get the event where Woytinsky proposes the concept in order to support it. The event is dynamic, and can trigger depending on factors such as: the state of the economy, deflation, labor faction strength, and most importantly internal party dissent. Appointing Woytinsky as an advisor aids significantly, as his presence passively increases the rate.

Dynamic mode is the intended way to play the mod, combining elements of both easy and historical modes. It reduces RNG with the shuffle leadership and card dismissal features of easy mode while retaining the starting variables of historical mode, such as relations and Reichsbanner strength.
You will have to get Stegerwald as the leader of Prussia, either through Braun resigning, or having a right-wing coalition form.
How do I cross the rubicon?

content: Hindenburg needs to dismiss Chancellor Brüning following the 1932 Presidential elections. This unlocks Rubicon Mode, which remains active for the rest of the game. Since this is the historical sequence of events, you'll need to follow a similar political path, such as securing a Hugenberg-led <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
, to have a better chance of unlocking it.

content.content: Why is the left path so hard?

content: Unlike Redux, this mod does not include any post–civil war content or additional <span style="color: #700000;">

or revolutionary paths. This is primarily due to time constraints—by the time of release, the mod had already been in development for over 9 months. As a result, the only truly "viable" path is the Reformist one, given the immense difficulty of building socialism within a bourgeois democracy—especially with figures like Hindenburg as president and the hostility of the bourgeois parties.

content.content: Why can't I form a coalition with a moderate Christian-Socialist DNVP or KVP?

The Christian Socials of the DNVP, and the party as a whole, remain a racist and antisemitic party, though they are more willing to operate within a democratic framework. The "Christian Socialism" of Weimar Germany is not the Christian Socialism of today; a better comparison would be Austria’s Christian Social Party. It is a nationalist, corporatist, and deeply religious right-wing ideology. The KVP is still a strongly anti-Marxist and nationalistic party at heart, and it would be against everything they stand for to coalition with the socialists.

His aim is to implement a new constitution via plebiscite—or, perhaps, simply through a presidential decree, with Hindenburg’s continued support.

Amid rising labor protests and growing hostility from all corners of German society, Schleicher can no longer support his former ally. Papen’s reckless pursuit of political suicide, backed only by President Hindenburg, has pushed Schleicher to distance himself from Papen’s unpopular policies in preparation for his own chancellorship. He has engaged with trade unions and a variety of political figures, including Gregor Strasser, to build the necessary support.
One thing is clear: Papen must go for German democracy to survive.

The treaty defines a formal relationship between the Church and the German state, guaranteeing freedom of worship for Catholics, and the right of the church to appoint their own clergy. Catholics in Germany are pleased, as are their representatives in the Center Party.

content: Following the Camarilla’s meeting with Papen and

content.content: The course Schleicher pursues is one of three options developed by his colleagues in the Defense Ministry. The first two involve unconstitutional maneuvers: either postponing elections or forcing the Reichstag into indefinite adjournment.

content: The third option, however, is more intriguing—a constructive vote of no confidence. Legal advisors have identified a loophole in the Republic’s constitution: while a hostile Reichstag majority can pass a no-confidence vote, it cannot unite to support a new cabinet. In the event of <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

content.content: To remedy this, the Defense Ministry proposes a constitutional amendment requiring the Reichstag to propose a viable replacement cabinet alongside any no-confidence motion—thereby curbing purely negative obstruction.

content: This option is favored within the Defense Ministry: it has the potential to attract republican support and avoid the civil unrest that the other two would likely provoke. Schleicher could remain in office as a caretaker indefinitely.

content.content: A precedent has even been set in Württemberg, where the Bolz government ignored a no-confidence vote from a purely negative majority and continued to rule by decree.

content: Crucially, this approach requires nothing from Hindenburg beyond passive acquiescence.

Though too late to save Schleicher’s tenure, it is approved by the chancellor and signed by Hindenburg without objection. The plan allocates half a billion marks to infrastructure projects across the Reich.
In the coming months, as millions of unemployed Germans return to work, it is not Schleicher, but his successor, who will reap the political rewards.

The Reichsbank, long known for its strict fiscal conservatism and obsessive anti-inflation stance, had already slashed Schleicher's initial public works decree by 15%. So, it was no surprise when news of even greater government spending met with their disapproval.

However, the endorsement of the campaign by Hjalmar Schacht—a respected banker and recently retired Reichsbank President credited with ending hyperinflation—has done much to calm the business community. Under government pressure, the Reichsbank is ultimately coerced into backing the plan, though not without forcing another 20% cut in funding.

Adam Stegerwald at the Labor Ministry, working closely with Günther Gereke, has been formulating a massive billion-mark public works program to expand on Schleicher’s previously modest efforts. They recognize that large-scale public projects and state spending are Germany’s path out of the slump—and Schleicher is eager to approve more to propel the nation back to great power status.

However, the chancellor has been persistently pressing his ministers to focus on rearmament and infrastructure that would support it—such as the construction of the Autobahn, a new nationwide highway system, and state funding for armament companies. To Schleicher’s frustration, however, most of the funds will still be directed toward civilian development.

ending_slides.weimar_win_a.title: Subending A - The World's Most Unstable Republic

content: The political deadlock that defined the gravest crisis of the Weimar Republic has persisted over the years. The

has never been fully reconciled with a system it was fundamentally opposed to from the start. Meanwhile, the estrangement of the Center Party from the Weimar Coalition has only deepened right-wing hostility toward the
The presidency has remained out of reach for the <span style="color: #c00000;">

, with successors to Hindenburg's worldview continuing to preside over Germany and obstruct our return to executive power. In 1939, a recession—sparked by European instability and rising tensions with the Soviet Union—triggered another wave of extremism. The Reichswehr was forced to step in to prevent a "March on Berlin" by both communists and fascism.
Though real democracy was formally restored in the 1960s following massive public discontent, the <span style="color: #6A1E1E;">
has remained a persistent force on the far-right. Recently rebranding itself as the
, it has capitalized on growing public anger over a refugee crisis driven by continued war and instability across Africa.

content.content: Ludwig Kaas has never truly embraced his role as party chairman, viewing it as a burden. He was elected as a compromise candidate, without actively campaigning for the position. Privately, he has made no secret of his desire to be relieved of the party chairmanship. With the stabilization of the Weimar Republic, Kaas believes he can retire without facing any significant consequences.

Despite pleads from his party members and colleagues, Kaas has officially resigned as head of the Center Party. This decision will have little impact, as he spent most of his time in Rome anyway, delegating the management of the party to his allies Joos and Brüning. No other Center member has missed as many Reichstag sessions as Kaas. Now, the party must find a successor, with potential candidates being his deputy leader Joos, Brüning, Stegerwald, or perhaps another compromise candidate.

content.content: The Nazis' rise is unprecedented for a political party in modern Germany, and socialist intellectuals are doing their best to come to terms with the rapid rise of this dangerous party.

The trade union researcher Theodor Geiger has written an article titled "Panik im Mittelstand", in which he describes the Nazis as being primarily a movement of the middle class, especially lower-middle civil servants and professionals who fear the proletarianizing effects of the Depression. Geiger argues that the middle class has been economically and politically unmoored, long split between many competing parties, squeezed between the big businesses and the proletariat. The mix of nationalist, anti-democratic, and loosely anti-capitalist rhetoric of the Nazis appeals to this group, perhaps only temporarily before the middle class discovers its true class interests.

By contrast, the theoretician Alexander Schifrin understands the Nazis as a new, unprecedented type of political movement, a fascist party that has non-economic appeal across class lines. He calls to attention its use of violent propaganda and street demonstrations as central to their rise.

Carlo Mierendorff, a leader of the "new revisionists", understands the Nazis as a politically incoherent but nevertheless powerful movement. They are kept together by the strength of their organizing machine and the emotional appeal of their nebulous ideology, which is able to attract less informed voters who voted based on feeling. Countering them would require a new style of campaigning, focused more on symbols and emotion rather than reason.
It is possible that all or none of these hypotheses are correct. Whatever the case, there must be something we can do to stop their rise.

content.content: At the turn of the decade, the Great Depression and widespread disillusionment with the Weimar system left few optimists in Germany. content: Brüning's days are numbered. The only reason President Hindenburg is keeping him around is solely by the fact of his foreign policy expertise, and his claim that he's only 'one hundred meters from the finish line' from achieving a huge breakthrough in terms of securing an abolishment of reparations at Lausanne and Germany's rearmament at Geneva, an issue close to Hindenburg's heart. The only hope for Brüning's political salvation rests in those conferences.

content.content: There is also no precedent of the President sacking a government that still enjoys a parliamentary majority.

However, General Kurt von Schleicher sees Brüning as the biggest obstacle in his 'taming strategy', as Brüning has refused to take serious efforts toward bringing the national opposition into government. The sense of urgency Schleicher has invoked onto the issue, along with his convincing of Hindenburg's State Secretary Otto Meissner and his son Oskar, has brought Hindenburg to make an early and rash decision on the matter.

It seems like this decision wasn't a rash one, but rather a matter of finding the appropriate pretext to dismiss our government.

The SPD remaining electorally resilient despite the radicalizing effects of the economic depression has thwarted Hindenburg’s plan to burden us with governance and erode our popularity. Realizing his strategy has failed, he now moves to dismiss us from government to prevent further socialist reforms from fueling our rising support.
Germany's economic crisis and our inadequate response have severely tested Hindenburg's patience, as he favors an austerity-driven approach.
The rapid rise of the far-right in local elections has pushed Hindenburg to appoint a government more in line with the national mood.
Kurt von Schleicher and the Reichswehr, outraged by our actions, have leveraged their influence over Hindenburg to push for our removal.
Business leaders, frustrated by our policies, have pressured Hindenburg’s inner circle to act against us.
This is a blatant violation of democracy, but we are powerless to stop it. Our only hope is to rally enough support in the next election to reclaim our mandate.

content.content: Chancellor Kurt von Schleicher claims to have a plan to save Germany, and he has reached out to the Social Democrats with vague promises. He claims that in order to govern, the Reichstag must be temporarily suspended to prevent the Nazis and Communists from disrupting government, in effect giving him and Hindenburg dictatorial powers. In the meantime, he is enacting a public works program and job creation plan, which he claims will stabilize the economy,

The trade unions are somewhat favorable to Schleicher's plan, as they see a commonality between Schleicher's economic plan and the ADGB's WTB-plan for debt-funded job creation. However, the rest of our party is vehemently against Schleicher.

Rumors are that Schleicher is also reaching out to the Nazis with similar promises of cooperation; he seems to believe that he can "tame" the Nazis. Most in our party do not trust him to not bring the Nazis to power. In addition, working with him would essentially mean the end of our claim to be a "democratic" party.

content.content: The Brüning cabinet has introduced the Eastern Aid Act, a policy aimed at relieving the debts of agricultural enterprises in the east—despite the significant financial burden it imposes. This measure directly contradicts Brüning’s broader strategy of economic recovery through budget austerity. To partially fund the policy, the government has retained outdated reparation taxes that became obsolete after the Young Plan. However, the lack of full funding for debt relief has frustrated many influential landowners, prompting them to take their complaints directly to Hindenburg, over whom they wield considerable influence.

content.content: The Brüning cabinet has introduced the Eastern Aid Act, a policy aimed at relieving the debts of agricultural enterprises in the east—despite the significant financial burden it imposes. This measure directly contradicts Brüning’s broader strategy of economic recovery through budget austerity. To partially fund the policy, the government has retained outdated reparation taxes that became obsolete after the Young Plan. However, the lack of full funding for debt relief has frustrated many influential landowners, prompting them to take their complaints directly to Hindenburg, over whom they wield considerable influence.

Brüning’s decision to sideline the Reichstag and its parties from any meaningful role in shaping his fiscal and economic policies severely undermined the legitimacy of the bourgeois parties in the eyes of their traditional electorates, due to their powerlessness to dismantle his more repugnant policies. One clear example is the plight of civil servants, who have borne the brunt of salary cuts of approximately 20 percent, pushing many toward the Nazis. His deflationary and austerity measures deepened the economic crisis, radicalizing the very social groups upon which these moderate parties relied for electoral support. This has led to heightened tensions between Brüning and his supporting parties, some of whom are even threatening to abandon his coalition.

content.content: The formation of the Austro-German customs union has prompted France to exert significant economic pressure on Austria. Leveraging its sizable influence over the Austrian economy, France is not only refusing to extend financial assistance to the country’s struggling major banks but is also deliberately withdrawing large sums of money, further destabilizing Austria's financial sector.

The major Austrian Bank Creditanstalt has declared bankruptcy, following French political and economic pressures aimed at undermining the plans for the Austro-German customs union. In that respect, they have certainly succeeded. We can only hope that this crisis does not spill over into Germany or, worse, spread across Europe.

content: Following Creditanstalt's bankruptcy, an event that has shaken international financial markets, investors are now rapidly withdrawing funds from German banks. Germany's heavy reliance on short-term foreign loans has turned Austria’s banking crisis into a direct threat to our own stability. In response, Reichsbank President

has implemented measures to curb capital flight by disincentivizing the transfer of money abroad. However, the effectiveness of these policies remains uncertain, and may cause unintended consequences.

content.content: Rumors have circulated regarding Center Party leader Ludwig Kaas's intention to resign, as he has privately expressed a desire to step down from his burdensome position. His frequent absences from Germany, often spent in Rome, have left his deputy leader Joos and parliamentary leader Brüning to effectively manage the party. Kaas also holds one of the worst attendance records in the Reichstag. However, Kaas has attributed his prolonged absences to poor health, and the considerable autonomy he has granted to his colleagues has quelled efforts to replace him with a more active, though controversial, leader.

Great Britain has abandoned the Gold Standard! The short-lived naval mutiny, caused by pay cuts, led to panic on the London Stock Exchange and a run on the Pound. The British government then adopted this policy as a means to stimulate industrial exports without the harmful side effects of deflation, achieved through the devaluation of the Pound. Germany's top economic experts viewed this as an act of desperation that would ruin England’s banks and insurance companies. Germany's citizens' fear of inflation, along with the obligation to preserve the mark’s value at 0.358 grams of fine gold under the Young Plan, has prevented Reichsbank President

from abandoning the Gold Standard. However, with both the United States and Britain showing sympathies toward our request for more flexible regulations, perhaps this decision was ultimately made on economic grounds after all.

, despite its critical lack of funds, stands the most resolute in its defense of the Weimar Republic, even more so than the Center Party. Meanwhile, the
has been drawn closer to Papen, as dictated by the terms of their alliance. The lines between the two parties are increasingly blurred, and a
member even resigned in protest over Dingeldey's refusal to take the final step and merge with the

Rumors suggest Chancellor Papen has secured the support of his cabinet and President Hindenburg for a decree authorizing a Reichsexekution against Prussia, justifying it with a fabricated claim of a merger between the
—a lie apparently convincing enough to sway Hindenburg. It seems all it takes is a pretext for him to present the already signed decree.
An immediate legal challenge has been launched against Papen's seizure of the Prussian government, with <span style="color: #c00000;">

and Center Party officials requesting an interim injunction to block Papen and his appointed commissioners from assuming control. The reactionary court has rejected the injunction, and the main proceedings are scheduled to begin only after a three-month delay.

content.content: Chancellor Papen has ordered the German delegation to walk out of the Geneva Disarmament Conference after France issued a strong objection to Germany’s demand for equal armament rights. Papen declared that Germany will not return to the conference unless the other powers agree to his terms.

The new right-wing and non-partisan Prussian cabinet assembled by Reichskommissar Papen has launched a large-scale purge of socialist and democratic officials from the civil service, forcing them into early retirement. Most of their replacements are conservatives—many of them nationalists. The purge is particularly aimed at socialist provincial presidents and police officials. An estimated 69 republican officials have been stripped of their power. Safe to say, the democratic bulwark has been dismantled.

content: % of the Reichstag due to its disadvantage from the lack of an electoral alliance, has sparked another round of debates over the party's continued existence. Resignation over the party's future is particularly strong within the business wing, with many members giving in to pressure to push for dissolution.

content.content: Even Dietrich has given up, announcing his resignation, but no one is willing to replace him.

content: However, the party's active state organizations in their strongholds of Baden-Württemberg and Hamburg manage to persuade the party against dissolution. As a result, the party has adopted a more energetic tone, with power shared among Dietrich, the energetic Württemberg minister Reinhold Maier, and Hamburg Mayor Carl Petersen—the former chairman of the <span style="color: #D3C24D;">

content.content: Perhaps the global recovery is finally on the horizon. Many economists now believe the slump has bottomed out, with the Frankfurt stock exchange climbing steadily—share and bond values have risen by over 30% since spring. But this resurgence remains abstract to the millions of unemployed Germans still trapped in poverty.

content: The aftermath of the Reichstag elections and the emergence of a Black-Brown majority has initiated negotiations between the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
and the Center Party. The latter hopes to restrain the Nazis by compelling a potential Chancellor
to govern through parliament rather than by decree. In doing so, he would be forced to consult a more conservative and dependable non-Nazi cabinet—where real power would reside.
General Schleicher has presented an enticing proposal to

, suggesting the formation of a presidential cabinet that would rule by decree. In this arrangement, Gregor Strasser would serve as Interior Minister of both Prussia and the Reich, while Schleicher believes he can control the Nazis by taking the role of Defense Minister. However, the Nazi leadership's enthusiasm quickly fades when President Hindenburg refuses to appoint
as Chancellor. Papen, deeply offended by Schleicher's apparent willingness to abandon him, has used his growing rapport with Hindenburg to undermine Schleicher’s influence over the President.
Following the results of the Reichstag elections, Papen and President Hindenburg met with
to hear his demands for the party’s participation in government.

requested to be appointed chancellor once again—a demand Hindenburg refused. Buoyed by their electoral triumph, the Nazis have now officially reneged on their earlier promises to tolerate Papen. Going forward, they will pursue an all-or-nothing strategy: the chancellorship for
Papen has released the contents of last week's conversations with

stormed into Hindenburg’s office to demand “total power over the state”—a violent one-party dictatorship—and was met with an angry rebuff from the president. This press release signals aims to signal the start of a counter-offensive against the Nazis. But now, no party is willing—or able—to follow the chancellor into open confrontation with the extremists. Even the Center Party finds
’s version of events more credible than Papen’s.
Coalition talks between the Center Party and
have continued, putting pressure on Papen to outmaneuver his former party in gaining the favor of the Nazis. Brüning, with permission from his party's leadership, has meet with the
's Strasser, promising support if he could convince
to govern via a parliamentary cabinet with Schleicher as Defense Minister and Goerdeler as the commissioner of Prussia.
Under pressure from their principal patron, General von Schleicher, the <span style="color: #0087DC;">

is compelled to support the unpopular Papen government—or risk losing Schleicher’s covert Reichswehr funding. Outraged by the party's backing of such an anti-social chancellor, the Christian Socials resign their positions in protest.
A follow-up meeting to last week’s discussion about a potential Black-Brown alliance, set up by Strasser, has resulted in
agreeing to delay the vote of no confidence against Papen.
also appeared to agree with Brüning’s other demands. Closer cooperation is expected in the near future, if both parties are genuine in their commitment to govern together via parliament.

content.content: Austria has obtained a League of Nations loan that is tied to a 20-year ban on Anschluss, but opposition from the Social Democrats and Greater German Party has stalled the law, before it finally is passed by a single vote.

content: The coalition talks between the Center Party and
have been called off, as Brüning grows increasingly uneasy about the grave risks involved. This decision is also influenced by his friend and our party member, Hilferding, who argued that the

would never restore parliamentary government. Hilferding also pointed out that many of Brüning's own party colleagues have fallen under Nazi influence, a fact confirmed when they all but agreed to impeach President Hindenburg in the planned deal. Hilferding also remains the only one in our party to advocate for toleration of Papen's cabinet as the only means to prevent a Nazi dictatorship. Brüning's goal is now to persuade the Nazis to give the Papen government 'a fair chance' to revive the economy.
The Center Party and its grassroots supporters are becoming increasingly demoralized, largely due to Brüning’s semi-secret negotiations with the

. Locally, party activists have faced the Nazis as violent thugs, disrupting rallies and intimidating opponents—far from the image of a potential coalition partner. Some activists are even taking up arms in self-defense, losing faith in their party and its leadership.

has publicly opposed the party’s recent vote of no confidence and the snap elections it triggered, warning that such moves would only erode the Nazis’ popular support and squander their only real chance to seize power. In response, an unofficial faction of about sixty Nazi Reichstag deputies has coalesced around Strasser—disillusioned by

content.content: General elections were held in Sweden, resulting in a great victory for Per Albin Hansson and his Social Democrats, who now govern in a minority government. The Swedish Social Democrats have embraced the concept of a 'people's home', a form of reformist socialism aimed at reducing class divides while working in the capitalist framework. Perhaps we should consider following their 'nordic' model?

The main proceedings in the case against Papen’s unconstitutional Reichsexekution of the Prussian government have begun, with a verdict expected in the coming weeks. Yet, the historically reactionary leanings of the judiciary place us at a clear disadvantage—despite support from the state governments of Bavaria and Baden, who have joined us in challenging the decree’s legality.

Chancellor of Austria Engelbert Dollfuß has used the "War Economy Enabling Act", a law passed during the days of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which allowed him to restructure the Creditanstalt without parliamentary approval. While the Austrian Social Democrats have protested, Dollfuß' actions are technically legal.

content: , in an attempt to revive their poll numbers, have outlined the concept of "national democracy," aiming to rekindle the nationalistic impulse that played such a crucial role in the German liberal movement. However, it is essentially a restatement of classical liberal ideology, tailored to appeal to a more nationalistic German middle class. The national democracy program also reaffirms the
's commitment to the Weimar Republic and recommends constitutional changes to strengthen it.
With its electoral alliance with the DNVP, the
's freedom of action has become increasingly constrained. Their rhetoric is aligning more closely with the
, now calling for the "liquidation of the Weimar system," an authoritarian overhaul of its constitution, and the withdrawal of power away from the masses.
Dingeldey and his associates are no longer content with merely renewing their electoral list connection with the <span style="color: #3E88B3;">
. Instead, they pushed for a unified Rechtsblock of the

, and various industrialist and business organizations to provide cohesive support for Hindenburg and Papen. However, Hugenberg has shown utter indifference, refusing to commit to anything beyond a renewal of the electoral list connection.
President Hindenburg has once again attempted to sound out the Nazis after the recent election results, with
signaling his readiness to seek the support of other parties if he were to be made chancellor first. Calling
's bluff, the president offered to appoint him, but only if he could secure a working majority in the Reichstag and allow the president to pick the defense and foreign ministers himself. As expected,
declined Hindenburg's proposal and suggested instead that, with emergency powers, he could form a satisfactory government in no time. Convinced that
sought nothing less than a presidential chancellorship, Hindenburg withdrew him from consideration.
Following another disastrous result for the <span style="color: #D3C24D;">
, a group of six former Reichstag deputies and high-ranking party members informed

that if a party congress—specifically meant to dissolve the party—isn't held, they would leave. However, this call has not gained much support, and Carl Petersen, former <span style="color: #D3C24D;">
chairman, has used his mediation skills to prevent the dissidents from publicly announcing their break with the party.

content.content: Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt has defeated incumbent Republican President Herbert Hoover in a landslide in the United States presidential election. This is attributed by the Great Depression and Roosevelt's campaigning for a "New Deal", proposing expansive public works and government reform.
Rumors are circulating widely that General Schleicher intends to undermine the very chancellor he helped install. Among his contacts, he's already being referred to as the chancellor-designate.

content: to make one final attempt at forming a majority coalition. Reporting back the next day,
confirmed that no such majority could be assembled. His recommendation was blunt: the only way forward is for the President to dismiss Papen, as the Reichstag will never accept him as chancellor.

has suffered yet another crushing setback—this time in the local elections in Thuringia. The results show the party lost nearly a quarter of its vote share compared to the previous state election. While low turnout may be a factor, this and three other recent local elections have only reinforced the growing sense that the Nazis have peaked and are rapidly losing support.

content.content: Despite his ousting, Papen remains in far closer physical proximity to the President than the chancellor does. At Hindenburg’s personal request, he continues to reside in an apartment within the Interior Ministry building—just steps from Hindenburg’s own quarters—while Schleicher lives miles away in a private residence. This arrangement has enabled Papen to scheme full-time, without attracting public attention.

Once a close ally, Oskar von Hindenburg has become an implacable enemy of the new chancellor—reportedly over a tasteless joke that wounded his pride beyond forgiveness. In Prussian times, such insults could end in duels; this time, the fallout may claim the life of the Republic. Two members of the Camarilla now harbor intense hostility toward Schleicher, and are working to sway the President into reconsidering his appointment.

Shortly after Schleicher’s appointment, the Western Allies, following protracted negotiations at the Geneva Disarmament Conference, conceded in principle to Germany’s right to equality in arms. The practical terms of this concession remain unclear, but in Schleicher’s view, it opens the path toward establishing an official militia service.

During Schleicher's addresses to the nation, one central theme rings clear: "Create Work!" He has revived efforts to resettle the urban unemployed on rural homesteads carved from bankrupt estates in the sparsely populated East. Although the Reichstag remains dissolved and he cannot legislate, he has publicly opposed Papen’s changes to the unemployment insurance system, presenting himself as a proponent of neither capitalism nor socialism. His ideological ambiguity has earned him the nickname "social general"—a label he embraces, claiming it aligns with the army’s tradition of solidarity between officers and soldiers.

content: 's resurgence in the polls has led Dingeldey to become overconfident, unequivocally supporting Papen, then Schleicher, and even forming a parliamentary faction with the various splinter parties between it and the
. While this move has bolstered their influence, it has alienated Hugenberg and the
, on whom they still depend on as of their electoral alliance.
For some odd reason, von Schleicher came to believe that nothing came of
’s attempts to be appointed parliamentary chancellor simply because the man didn’t “at the bottom of his heart” want the office. By

, this suspicion had become a firm conviction; he repeatedly confided to journalists and his cabinet that the man simply doesn’t really want power. This belief is leading to Schleicher overestimating his chances of securing <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
Heavy electoral losses for the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">

in local elections have further reinforced the disillusionment of the voters who have brought the movement to prominence, many who joined and donated to the party expecting to receive the spoils of victory are beginning to despair, withdrawing their donations. Admission fees for rallies, once a major source of income at the local level, have collapsed despite steep price reductions.

's failure to gain the chancellorship or enter government to constructively relieve Germany's economic woes has caused further frustration among the movement. However, Nazi leaders are quick to suppress any leaks of dissent or rumors of decline to the public.
The global economy is on the upswing—and with it, the erosion of the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
continues. The republican police force surveilling the

in Munich has noted clear signs of disintegration. Resignations are occurring daily, membership dues arrive irregularly, and expulsions over indebtedness are increasingly common. Every branch of the party appears run down. As for morale, the police report observed: “The view that the peak has passed and favorable prospects are missed is commonly held among many members.”
Schleicher still clings to the illusionary hope that the now powerless Strasser might somehow persuade
to allow Nazi participation in his cabinet, now that Strasser has returned from vacation. Strasser’s absence from the public eye has unsettled

, who now fears potential backroom plots to fracture the party—especially given the eagerness of Strasser’s remaining loyalists to do just that. In reality, all Strasser does is to warn former chancellor Brüning that Papen has arranged a secret meeting with Hitler—set to take place within a week or two—to conspire against their mutual enemy: Schleicher.

's financial situation is becoming dire. Increasingly, equipment and supplies are being acquired on credit—credit that's already drying up under the weight of the party's existing debts. Tensions have begun to flare between the

and the party leadership over how to divide dwindling donations, with some members resorting to begging in the streets or organizing lotteries to scrape together funds. One more election, and the party could face a full-blown financial crisis.

Despite promising President Hindenburg not to publicly criticize his favored former chancellor, Schleicher has done just that in a bid to distance himself from the deeply unpopular Papen. Hindenburg, displeased by the breach of trust, grows increasingly estranged from Schleicher. Papen, for his part, has shown little outward hostility toward his ouster—carefully masking his resentment and thirst for revenge beneath a façade of cordiality. In the meantime, Hindenburg has quietly authorized him to serve as his secret liaison to

content.content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has grown frustrated with the chancellor after a request for intervention to clear bureaucratic obstacles was flatly rejected. His ambitious projects remain stalled. Gereke, disillusioned, has confided his disappointment to his close friend—none other than Oskar von Hindenburg.

content: Günther Gereke, the energetic special commissioner for public works, has had his project accelerated after his request for the chancellor to intervene and clear bureaucratic obstacles was approved.

vote share among radicalized workers, has motivated the move.

content.content: The disastrous state of the German economy has made rearmament a pipe dream, and Schleicher is eager to get it back on track.

The campaign for the Landtag elections in the microscopically small Free State of Lippe has begun, with the Nazis investing a substantial amount of resources to sway just a hundred thousand voters. However, despite its small size, a victory here could dispel the growing belief that the Nazis are on the brink of a catastrophic decline.

content: At a private dinner with journalists, Chancellor von Schleicher repeatedly expressed confidence that the Nazi leader would eventually come around to tolerating his cabinet—despite

’s public affirmations of an all-or-nothing course. This, even as Schleicher made clear he would dissolve the Reichstag if needed, a move he believes would cost the Nazis further seats (though he seeks to avoid such a step, fearing the
would benefit most from their collapse). “They’ll soon be eating out of my hand,” were the chancellor’s exact words that evening. What Schleicher fails to grasp is that
is no ordinary politician. He will not respond rationally, nor prudently, to Strasser’s break or to the <span style="color: #7A3C00;">
’s electoral collapse. He believes destiny is on his side.

Chancellor von Schleicher and his press secretary have deliberately “leaked” plans to appoint Strasser as Vice Chancellor, Interior Minister, and Minister-President of Prussia, alongside naming the Center Party labor leader Stegerwald as Labor Minister. The Agriculture and Economics Ministries were reportedly reserved for Hugenberg himself. It’s highly likely this is a bluff—an attempt to pressure the
into dropping its total opposition, lest they risk being sidelined entirely.
With Dingeldey's pretentiousness, fueled by the <span style="color: #C0A054;">

's uptick in polling, elevating it to the lead party on the "moderate" Right, Hugenberg is growing increasingly irritated by their independence and seeks to terminate their electoral alliance if new elections are called. While the
still hopes to renew the alliance, they begin exploring the possibility of an accommodation with the

and the bourgeois parties as a safeguard against near-certain annihilation if Hugenberg severs ties. Meanwhile, the DNV (German National Association), a non-partisan organization aiming to consolidate the German middle, is starting to repair its relations with the liberals after already securing the support of the non-liberal right, with politicians like Treviranus.

content.content: Von Schleicher's bluffs—such as proposing a cabinet that includes both Stegerwald and Hugenberg—have lost all credibility. The Center Party has publicly ruled out Stegerwald serving alongside Hugenberg, a notorious enemy of organized labor. Moreover, the leak about the President’s meeting with Strasser has led to a permanent break between the Nazi leader and Schleicher, ending any hope that Strasser might persuade him to support a cabinet involving Schleicher. His contradictory tactics and careless remarks have only deepened mistrust and furthered his political isolation. He only now condemns efforts to postpone elections—despite having supported the idea just a week earlier.

With progress stalled across nearly all sectors, Schleicher has attempted to shift focus by bringing the issue of rearmament back into the public eye. He announced plans to establish a compulsory militia within a year, alongside a renewed commitment to arming the Reichswehr with heavy weaponry and instituting universal conscription. However, the impact of this intended public relations triumph is minimal, as news of Schleicher’s political setbacks dominates public attention.

Having failed to extract concessions from the chancellor to turn Germany into a dictatorship, the more radical elements within his party have pressured him into adopting an all-out opposition to Schleicher. A strongly worded resolution has been released, accusing him of "vacillation" in his willingness to "reform" the constitution. Furthermore, his initiative to restart peasant homesteads on bankrupt eastern estates has drawn the ire of conservative elites. With the next vote of no confidence looming, it may well come down to Schleicher versus the entire chamber.

Dollfuß has abused his powers given in the "War Economy Enabling Act" to crack down on the workers in a railroad strike, which has resulted in all three presidents of parliament resigning amid a crucial vote. This crisis presented a perfect opportunity for Dollfuß to abolish the parliamentary system and restrict democratic rights, such as the freedom of the press and public protests. Another democracy has fell to authoritarianism.

Dollfuß's Austrofascist dictatorship has banned the Austrian Communists and the paramilitary of the Austrian Social Democrats, the Republican Protection League. He has also established the Fatherland Front, a party promoting a far-right fascist and corporate ideology.

content.content: The Austrian Civil War has begun and ended in a matter of three days, fought between the Republican Protection League and Austria's Austrofascist regime, resulting in a defeat for the socialists across the border. The uprising was sparked by efforts to suppress the remnants of the Austrian Social Democrats and their paramilitary wing. However, the poorly coordinated and weakened movement was swiftly crushed by the army. Perhaps things would have gone more differently if they have taken up arms earlier.

content.content: According to the Constitution, women are equal to men, but this is not followed in practice. Women in the workforce are not paid equally for the same work, in addition to often being pushed out of employment after marriage. Men are still favored in marriage and family policy, and there are restrictions on women's rights in many other domains. And that is not to mention the overwhelming patriarchal culture present in Germany.

content.content: Brüning himself continues to resist forming a more right-wing cabinet to appease the defectors, believing that at least one of them will waver in the face of the political and economic instability that would follow.

The national opposition remains committed to its all-or-nothing approach, refusing to support the government unless they are granted the Chancellery. Despite this, many on the Right still believe that a compromise with Hitler and Hugenberg is possible and believe that Brüning is not making enough of an effort to achieve it.

content.content: Education in Germany has traditionally been organized on religious and class lines. Schools are often either Protestant or Catholic (or rarely Jewish), and religious classes are required in most mixed-denomination schools. In addition, the working class has at most eight years of public education in primary and middle schools, while the middle and upper classes have access to private schools and Gymnasiums that prepare students for universities. Thus, the universities tend to be dominated by conservatives and reactionaries, which has negative consequences for bureaucratic recruitment.

content: After several rounds of elimination voting at the <span style="color: #00C0FF;">

’s inaugural congress, Oskar Hergt secured the chairmanship by uniting the party’s monarchist‑conservative wing. The moderate Frank Glatzel was the first to go, followed by Hans von Raumer, whose industrialist backers then fragmented between Treviranus and Hergt. In the penultimate round, Kuno von Westarp withdrew and threw his delegates behind Hergt rather than the centrist faction led by Gottfried Treviranus. Agrarian conservatives, church‑aligned delegates, and a sizable bloc of
conservatives gave him the edge over Treviranus in the final ballot.
Hergt’s victory has seen our relations with the <span style="color: #00C0FF;">

sour. His entrenched monarchism and hostility toward democratic processes have already led him to explore increased cooperation with the far right, including informal contacts with the Stahlhelm. Genuine legislative collaboration now seems all but impossible, making building coalitions in the future increasingly difficult.

content.content: The Center Party is internally split on this. Their ties to the Schleicher cabinet and the pro-Schleicher sentiment expressed by many of their party members have made joining the socialist-led boycott a hard pill to swallow. However, we have gained the sympathy of their left wing.

The Center Party is already a Blocpartei, so it's out of the question. However, we have some sympathetic voices on the party's left wing, like Wirth and Jakob Kaiser of the Christian labor unions, lending their support nonetheless.

With or without a strong campaign, we believe the wave of support we gained after toppling Schleicher’s regime will be enough to carry us to victory in the referendum. The Right remains too fractured to fully exploit our relative absence from the field—though we’ve begun to notice a troubling uptick in opposition activity, with expenses being covered by an unknown source.

schleicher_19.spd_med.title: Schleicher attempts to negotiate with us.

content.content: The nationwide general strike against Schleicher's authoritarian regime has brought the country to a standstill. The chancellor could unleash the Reichswehr and far-right paramilitaries to brutally crush the protests—but for now, that remains a last resort. Instead, Schleicher has chosen to open negotiations with the opposition.

Meanwhile, in defiance of the indefinite adjournment of the Reichstag, the republican parties have banded together to unofficially reconvene the chamber at a separate location, openly challenging federal authority.
However, perhaps we have overestimated our strength—strikes rarely last with unemployment so high, especially with Schleicher’s sympathizers embedded within the unions themselves.

content.content: But perhaps we can bypass this deadlock by targeting Hindenburg himself. With a two-thirds majority in the Reichstag, we could initiate impeachment proceedings under Article 59 or trigger a recall election under Article 43. If the recall election were to fail, the Reichstag would be dissolved for new elections.

Yet the reactionary nature of the courts renders impeachment unlikely to succeed. Recall, however, remains a narrow possibility—it requires only a majority of those who vote, not of all eligible voters. Still, to make either path viable, we must secure the backing of other parties.

The Reichsbank, long known for its strict fiscal conservatism and obsessive anti-inflation stance, had already slashed Schleicher's initial public works decree by 15%. So, it was no surprise when news of even greater government spending met with their disapproval.

However, the endorsement of the campaign by Hjalmar Schacht—a respected banker and former Reichsbank President credited with ending hyperinflation—has done much to calm the business community. Under government pressure, the Reichsbank is ultimately coerced into backing the plan.

content.content: Following a brief civil war between republican forces and the far-right, we’ve been given a blank slate to rebuild Germany on a truly democratic and social foundation—free, for now, from the fear of reactionary reprisals. A minor coup attempt by General Bredow is foiled, and with it, the Reichswehr is finally brought under the banner of the republic.

But it is not all sunshine and rainbows. The civil war has devastated countless lives, and the costs of reconstruction and welfare have triggered the return of hyperinflationary nightmares. Hunger now exceeds levels seen during the Great Depression, and many are already growing disillusioned with their supposed saviors. Though the reactionary and far-right forces were defeated on the battlefield, it's only a matter of years before a new right-wing movement emerges and takes root among the weary and discontented populace.

content.content: The League of Nations is hosting a conference to discuss the state of the global economy and potential solutions to the ongoing depression. All parties want to reduce tariffs to encourage trade. However, the Western powers are at an impasse; France and to a lesser extent Britain are calling for fixed currency exchange rates, while President Roosevelt of the United States wants to print new money to stimulate demand, calling for "controlled inflation". The Europeans want to reduce their debts to the US, while America favors continued full payments.

content.content: Schleicher has been working intensively over the past weeks to forge a formal alliance between the trade unions and the state, focusing his efforts on the Christian associations. content: Under this agreement, the blue-collar Hirsch-Duncker, Christian, and the Strasserist

unions are merged into the new German Labor Front (DAF). White-collar and civil servant unions, including the DHV, are folded into their own section within the Front. The right to strike is curtailed, and all members are made to pledge full loyalty to the so-called "national interest"—however the state chooses to define it.

content.content: Local union leaders who refuse to join are having their offices raided, their funds confiscated, and themselves imprisoned. While membership in the German Labor Front is technically voluntary, access to benefits—and even basic protections—is now locked behind it, making participation all but mandatory. Furthermore, a new department is established in the DAF, tasked solely with spreading state propaganda and binding the workers more tightly into the Volksgemeinschaft.
The chancellor is also able to palate the industrialists, by placing their power significantly above that of labor in the newly established corporatist framework.

With the Center Party already on the verge of breaking with Schleicher's cabinet after the unconstitutional adjournment of the chamber, this latest undemocratic act has convinced its leaders that only a united republican front can restore Germany to normalcy.

content.content: Our party is wracked as to how to deal with the economic crisis. From the centrist faction, Hilferding argues that the economic crisis must be allowed to play out, because it is simply a part of the cyclic nature of capitalism.

The Labor faction is arguing for increased welfare spending to alleviate the suffering of the workers. Their economist, Wladimir Woytinsky, has voiced support for a public works campaign involving deficit spending, but it will take time to iron out the details. Furthermore, he will need the united support of the ADGB; otherwise, he won't have the power to challenge Hilferding's stance.

From labor, the economist Wladimir Woytinsky argues that we must pursue a massive public works program to reduce unemployment and stimulate demand, perhaps including deficit spending. His opponents, like Hilferding, argue that this plan will cause a return to hyper-inflation, and that it would not even help the economy. In addition, according to Hilferding, Woytinsky's strategy is opposed to Marxist principles.
The so-called WTB plan, after its chief supporters Woytinsky, Tarnow, and Baade, is receiving more attention within the party.

However, leftists in the party argue that the WTB plan is merely a bandage over the fundamental flaws of capitalism. They argue that the crisis is an opportunity to end capitalism through massive nationalizations of industry, and finally bring our country to socialism.

Meanwhile, moderates and reformists draw up proposals for a limited plan of job creation through public works, funded through taxes, that does not involve deficit spending or large-scale restructuring of the economy. Labor argues that the plan is inadequate in its scale and ambition.

content.content: Despite the Republic’s paper victory, revanchist sentiment over the loss of Eastern and Western territories, coupled with mass radicalization from the staggering death toll, destruction, hyperinflation, widespread hunger, and the absence of meaningful foreign aid, has deeply discredited the political establishment. Under pressure from the Reichswehr, martial law remains in place for years, with the military increasingly intruding into civilian governance.

content: By 1939, a global recession—triggered by escalating instability across Europe and threats from the Soviet Union—obliterates the reconstruction progress made by the ruling

, plunging the country into yet another crisis. Following a March on Berlin, a "Third Positionist" regime seizes power, led by a new political party composed of former Nazis and disillusioned socialists.

content.content: Germany pivots toward autarky and radical self-reliance, sealing its borders to foreigners. The regime earns the moniker "Black Spot of Europe," ruling from 1940 to 1996. During this period, it successfully coerces the withdrawal of foreign troops from the Rhineland and reclaims its lost eastern territories—including the Polish Corridor—in 1946, capitalizing on Poland's distraction with the Soviet threat and the shifting priorities of the Western Allies as they fight war with Japan.

Today, Germany remains largely isolated from the rest of the world, with the successor to the dictatorship of old being not much better, being ruled by oligarchs and the wealthy who are relicts of the past regime. Now, the task of Social Democracy is to prepare for the next election. The incumbent government of Wolfgang Schäuble is unpopular, and we stand to gain. Perhaps the next government will have a socialist plurality.

The Hindenburg Mythos serves as a powerful rallying point for all parties, as he maintains high personal popularity despite everything Germany has endured. However, the more support he receives from the German left and center, the more Hindenburg views it as a stain on his personal honor. The refusal of August von Mackensen and other high-ranking officers with whom he served during the war to embrace his candidacy proved particularly painful to the Reich president.

In response, he may shift further to the right after the election in an effort to restore his sense of honor and to appease his former comrades and friends on the German Right. This urge has only been reinforced by the Harzburg Front’s refusal to support him without concessions, as they see Hindenburg as the greatest obstacle to their rise to power.

content: With the Nazi movement in decline following the end of the economic depression and an internal leadership struggle, and with the election of the nationalist Hergt alongside the appointment of the
